lessons.title: Introduction
teaches: Two players face each other across the board: White has the light pieces and Black the dark ones.
White always makes the first move, and then the players take turns.
Each player starts with sixteen pieces on a board of sixty-four squares.
The goal is checkmate: attacking the enemy king so that it has no escape.
The king is never captured; the game ends as soon as it is checkmated.

beats.label: Welcome to chess
beats.say: Welcome to chess, a game for two players. One player has the light pieces and is called White; the other has the dark pieces and is called Black.
beats.speak: Welcome to chess, a game for two players. One player has the light pieces and is called White; the other has the dark pieces and is called Black.

beats.label: Sixteen pieces each
beats.say: Each player starts with sixteen pieces. White's are lined up on the two rows nearest to White: eight pawns in front and eight larger pieces behind.
beats.speak: Each player starts with sixteen pieces. White's are lined up on the two rows nearest to White: eight pawns in front and eight larger pieces behind.

beats.label: Black's army
beats.say: Black's sixteen pieces stand the same way on the far side, facing White's army across the empty middle of the board.
beats.speak: Black's sixteen pieces stand the same way on the far side, facing White's army across the empty middle of the board.

beats.label: White moves first
beats.say: White always makes the first move of the game. Here White pushes the pawn in front of the queen two squares forward.
beats.speak: White always makes the first move of the game. Here White pushes the pawn in front of the queen two squares forward.

beats.label: Taking turns
beats.say: Then Black answers, pushing the pawn in front of Black's queen two squares forward. After that the turns alternate: White, Black, White, Black, one move at a time.
beats.speak: Then Black answers, pushing the pawn in front of Black's queen two squares forward. After that the turns alternate: White, Black, White, Black, one move at a time.

beats.label: No passing
beats.say: On your turn you must make exactly one move. You cannot skip a turn, and you cannot move twice in a row.
beats.speak: On your turn you must make exactly one move. You cannot skip a turn, and you cannot move twice in a row.

beats.label: The board
beats.say: The board has sixty-four squares in eight rows of eight, coloured light and dark. The Chessboard lesson shows how every square gets its name.
beats.speak: The board has sixty-four squares in eight rows of eight, coloured light and dark. The Chessboard lesson shows how every square gets its name.

beats.label: Six kinds of piece
beats.say: Each army has one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights and eight pawns. Every kind of piece moves in its own way.
beats.speak: Each army has one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights and eight pawns. Every kind of piece moves in its own way.

beats.label: The king
beats.say: The most important piece is the king. Each king starts in the middle of its back row, right beside its queen, facing the other king.
beats.speak: The most important piece is the king. Each king starts in the middle of its back row, right beside its queen, facing the other king.

beats.label: Capturing
beats.say: Usually, a piece captures by moving onto a square held by an enemy piece, which is then taken off the board. Here White's knight jumps onto a black pawn and captures it.
beats.speak: Usually, a piece captures by moving onto a square held by an enemy piece, which is then taken off the board. Here White's knight jumps onto a black pawn and captures it.

beats.label: The real goal
beats.say: Capturing pieces helps, but the real goal is the enemy king. Here White's rook attacks the black king along a straight, open line. An attacked king is said to be in check.
beats.speak: Capturing pieces helps, but the real goal is the enemy king. Here White's rook attacks the black king along a straight, open line. An attacked king is said to be in check.

beats.label: Escaping check
beats.say: A king in check must escape at once. This king can step to either side, off the rook's line, so the game goes on.
beats.speak: A king in check must escape at once. This king can step to either side, off the rook's line, so the game goes on.

beats.label: Checkmate
beats.say: Now White's rook slides all the way to the far corner and checks the black king. The king's own pawns block its way forward, and the rook covers the rest of that back row, so there is no escape.
beats.speak: Now White's rook slides all the way to the far corner and checks the black king. The king's own pawns block its way forward, and the rook covers the rest of that back row, so there is no escape.

beats.label: Checkmate wins
beats.say: A king in check with no way out is checkmated. Checkmate ends the game at once, and the player who gives it wins.
beats.speak: A king in check with no way out is checkmated. Checkmate ends the game at once, and the player who gives it wins.

beats.label: The king is never taken
beats.say: Notice that the king is never actually captured. The game is over the moment it is checkmated, so it never leaves the board.
beats.speak: Notice that the king is never actually captured. The game is over the moment it is checkmated, so it never leaves the board.

beats.label: Other endings
beats.say: Not every game ends in checkmate. A player may resign, which means giving up, and some games end in a draw, where nobody wins.
beats.speak: Not every game ends in checkmate. A player may resign, which means giving up, and some games end in a draw, where nobody wins.

beats.label: Where chess came from
beats.say: Chess grew from a game played in India about fifteen hundred years ago. It spread through Persia to Europe, where the rules we use today settled about five hundred years ago.
beats.speak: Chess grew from a game played in India about fifteen hundred years ago. It spread through Persia to Europe, where the rules we use today settled about five hundred years ago.

beats.label: What comes next
beats.say: Next, The Chessboard lesson teaches the name of every square, and then you will meet the pieces one by one.
beats.speak: Next, The Chessboard lesson teaches the name of every square, and then you will meet the pieces one by one.

lessons.title: The Chessboard
teaches: The board has sixty-four squares, alternating light and dark.
Each player has a light square in the right-hand corner nearest to them.
Files are the columns, lettered a to h; ranks are the rows, numbered 1 to 8.
To name a square, say its file letter first and then its rank number: e4, d6, h1.
Diagonals are slanting lines of squares that all share one colour.

beats.label: Sixty-four squares
beats.say: A chessboard has sixty-four squares, arranged in eight rows of eight.
beats.speak: A chessboard has sixty-four squares, arranged in eight rows of eight.

beats.label: Light and dark
beats.say: The squares are light and dark in turn, like a chequerboard. Two squares that share a side are never the same colour.
beats.speak: The squares are light and dark in turn, like a chequerboard. Two squares that share a side are never the same colour.

beats.label: Light square on the right
beats.say: Imagine you are playing White. Look at the corner nearest to you on your right: that square is light.
beats.speak: Imagine you are playing White. Look at the corner nearest to you on your right: that square is light.

beats.label: Black's corner too
beats.say: Black sits on the opposite side, facing White. Black's right-hand corner is this one, and it is light too. If the corner on your right is dark, turn the board.
beats.speak: Black sits on the opposite side, facing White. Black's right-hand corner is this one, and it is light too. If the corner on your right is dark, turn the board.

beats.label: Files
beats.say: The columns that run from White's side to Black's side are called files. There are eight, lettered a to h from White's left to White's right.
beats.speak: The columns that run from White's side to Black's side are called files. There are eight, lettered a to h from White's left to White's right.

beats.label: The e-file
beats.say: This highlighted column is the e-file. It runs all the way from White's side of the board to Black's.
beats.speak: This highlighted column is the e-file. It runs all the way from White's side of the board to Black's.

beats.label: Ranks
beats.say: The rows that run across the board are called ranks. There are eight, numbered 1 to 8, starting from White's side.
beats.speak: The rows that run across the board are called ranks. There are eight, numbered 1 to 8, starting from White's side.

beats.label: The fourth rank
beats.say: This highlighted row is the fourth rank. It is the fourth row up from White's side.
beats.speak: This highlighted row is the fourth rank. It is the fourth row up from White's side.

beats.label: Naming a square
beats.say: Every square is named by its file letter and then its rank number. The e-file and the fourth rank cross on this square, so it is called e4.
beats.speak: Every square is named by its file letter and then its rank number. The e-file and the fourth rank cross on this square, so it is called E four.

beats.label: Letter first, then number
beats.say: The file letter always comes first, in lower case: e4, never 4e or E4.
beats.speak: The file letter always comes first, in lower case: E four, never 4e or E4.

beats.label: Finding a square
beats.say: To find a square, go along to its file, then count up the ranks. For d6, find the d-file and count up: one, two, three, four, five, six.
beats.speak: To find a square, go along to its file, then count up the ranks. For D six, find the d-file and count up: one, two, three, four, five, six.

beats.label: The four corners
beats.say: The four corners are a1 and h1 on White's side, and a8 and h8 on Black's side.
beats.speak: The four corners are A one and H one on White's side, and A eight and H eight on Black's side.

beats.label: Naming a piece's square
beats.say: When a piece stands on a square, we use that square's name. This knight is on the c-file and the fifth rank, so it stands on c5.
beats.speak: When a piece stands on a square, we use that square's name. This knight is on the c-file and the fifth rank, so it stands on C five.

beats.label: Another one
beats.say: This black rook is on the g-file and the third rank. It stands on g3.
beats.speak: This black rook is on the g-file and the third rank. It stands on G three.

beats.label: Names stay the same
beats.say: Square names never change: a1 is always the corner on White's left, even when you play Black. At the start, White's pieces fill ranks 1 and 2, and Black's fill ranks 7 and 8.
beats.speak: Square names never change: A one is always the corner on White's left, even when you play Black. At the start, White's pieces fill ranks 1 and 2, and Black's fill ranks 7 and 8.

beats.label: Diagonals
beats.say: Squares also link corner to corner in slanting lines called diagonals. This long diagonal runs from a1 to h8, and every square on it is dark.
beats.speak: Squares also link corner to corner in slanting lines called diagonals. This long diagonal runs from A one to H eight, and every square on it is dark.

beats.label: A short diagonal
beats.say: Diagonals come in many lengths. This one has just three squares, f1, g2 and h3, and all three are light.
beats.speak: Diagonals come in many lengths. This one has just three squares, F one, G two and H three, and all three are light.

beats.label: One colour per diagonal
beats.say: A diagonal never changes colour. This one, from a6 down to f1, is light from one end to the other.
beats.speak: A diagonal never changes colour. This one, from A six down to F one, is light from one end to the other.

beats.label: The centre
beats.say: The four middle squares are d4, e4, d5 and e5. Together they are called the centre, and you will hear about them often.
beats.speak: The four middle squares are D four, E four, D five and E five. Together they are called the centre, and you will hear about them often.

beats.label: You can name any square
beats.say: Now you can name and find any square on the board. Next, you will meet the first piece: the pawn.
beats.speak: Now you can name and find any square on the board. Next, you will meet the first piece: the pawn.

lessons.title: The Pawn
teaches: Each player starts with eight pawns, on the second rank for White and the seventh rank for Black.
A pawn moves straight forward one square, and never backwards or sideways.
A pawn that has not moved yet may advance two squares, as long as both are empty.
A pawn captures one square diagonally forward, never straight ahead.
A pawn with a piece directly in front of it is blocked and cannot move forward.
A pawn is worth one point.

practice.goal: Move your pawns forward, capture with them when it is safe, and try to win the black pawns.
hints: Pawns move straight ahead but capture one square diagonally forward. Move a pawn up until it attacks a black pawn, and check that it will be safe there.
The black pawn on d5 is the nearest target: a white pawn on c4 or e4 would attack it.
practice.success: You moved a pawn forward and captured with a pawn. Play on and try to win the black pawns, keeping your own pawns safe.

beats.label: Meet the pawn
beats.say: Meet the pawn, the smallest member of each army. Every player starts the game with eight of them.
beats.speak: Meet the pawn, the smallest member of each army. Every player starts the game with eight of them.

beats.label: Where the pawns start
beats.say: White's eight pawns stand on the second rank, from a2 to h2. Black's eight pawns stand on the seventh rank, from a7 to h7.
beats.speak: White's eight pawns stand on the second rank, from A two to H two. Black's eight pawns stand on the seventh rank, from A seven to H seven.

beats.label: One step forward
beats.say: Pawns walk straight ahead, usually one square per move; there is one exception you will see soon. This white pawn steps from g3 to g4.
beats.speak: Pawns walk straight ahead, usually one square per move; there is one exception you will see soon. This white pawn steps from G three to G four.

beats.label: Never backwards
beats.say: A pawn can never move backwards or sideways. From g4 its only step is forward, to g5.
beats.speak: A pawn can never move backwards or sideways. From G four its only step is forward, to G five.

beats.label: Black's pawns face the other way
beats.say: For Black, forward means towards the first rank, on White's side. This black pawn steps from b7 to b6.
beats.speak: For Black, forward means towards the first rank, on White's side. This black pawn steps from B seven to B six.

beats.label: Two squares on the first move
beats.say: On its very first move, a pawn may go two squares instead of one. This pawn on d2 may step to d3 or go straight to d4.
beats.speak: On its very first move, a pawn may go two squares instead of one. This pawn on D two may step to D three or go straight to D four.

beats.label: The double step
beats.say: Here it takes the double step, from d2 to d4, passing over the empty square d3.
beats.speak: Here it takes the double step, from D two to D four, passing over the empty square D three.

beats.label: The double step is optional
beats.say: The double step is a choice, not a rule. This pawn moves just one square, from f2 to f3.
beats.speak: The double step is a choice, not a rule. This pawn moves just one square, from F two to F three.

beats.label: Only once
beats.say: Now that this pawn has moved, its chance for a double step is gone. From f3 it can only go to f4.
beats.speak: Now that this pawn has moved, its chance for a double step is gone. From F three it can only go to F four.

beats.label: A blocked pawn
beats.say: A pawn cannot jump over anything. The black knight on g3 stands right in front of this pawn, so the pawn cannot move at all.
beats.speak: A pawn cannot jump over anything. The black knight on G three stands right in front of this pawn, so the pawn cannot move at all.

beats.label: A blocked double step
beats.say: The double step needs both squares empty. This pawn may step to b3, but the black bishop on b4 stops it reaching b4.
beats.speak: The double step needs both squares empty. This pawn may step to B three, but the black bishop on B four stops it reaching B four.

beats.label: Capturing diagonally
beats.say: A pawn captures differently from the way it moves: one square diagonally forward. This pawn on g3 attacks the knight on h4.
beats.speak: A pawn captures differently from the way it moves: one square diagonally forward. This pawn on G three attacks the knight on H four.

beats.label: The capture
beats.say: The pawn takes the knight by moving from g3 to h4. The knight leaves the board, and the pawn stands in its place.
beats.speak: The pawn takes the knight by moving from G three to H four. The knight leaves the board, and the pawn stands in its place.

beats.label: Two attacked squares
beats.say: A pawn attacks the squares just ahead of it on each diagonal. This pawn on f4 attacks e5 and g5.
beats.speak: A pawn attacks the squares just ahead of it on each diagonal. This pawn on F four attacks E five and G five.

beats.label: No capturing straight ahead
beats.say: A pawn cannot capture straight ahead. These two pawns on c4 and c5 block each other, and neither of them can move.
beats.speak: A pawn cannot capture straight ahead. These two pawns on C four and C five block each other, and neither of them can move.

beats.label: A blocked pawn can capture
beats.say: A blocked pawn can still capture. When a black knight stands on b5, the white pawn takes it by moving from c4 to b5.
beats.speak: A blocked pawn can still capture. When a black knight stands on B five, the white pawn takes it by moving from C four to B five.

beats.label: No capturing backwards
beats.say: Pawns never capture backwards. The knights on c4 and e4 are behind the pawn on d5, so it cannot take them.
beats.speak: Pawns never capture backwards. The knights on C four and E four are behind the pawn on D five, so it cannot take them.

beats.label: Black captures too
beats.say: Black's pawns capture diagonally forward too, which for Black means towards the first rank. This black pawn takes the knight, moving from f5 to g4.
beats.speak: Black's pawns capture diagonally forward too, which for Black means towards the first rank. This black pawn takes the knight, moving from F five to G four.

beats.label: Worth one point
beats.say: A pawn is worth one point, the smallest value of any piece. Yet pawns standing side by side, or guarding each other, are hard to get past.
beats.speak: A pawn is worth one point, the smallest value of any piece. Yet pawns standing side by side, or guarding each other, are hard to get past.

beats.label: Try it yourself
beats.say: Your turn to practise. Each side has a king and four pawns; you take White against the computer. Move forward, capture diagonally, and keep your pawns safe.
beats.speak: Your turn to practise. Each side has a king and four pawns; you take White against the computer. Move forward, capture diagonally, and keep your pawns safe.

lessons.title: Pawn Duel
teaches: Pawn Duel uses six pawns each, from b2 to g2 for White and from b7 to g7 for Black.
White moves first, and the pawns move and capture just as in a real game.
You win by reaching the far rank, by capturing every opposing pawn, or when your opponent has no move.
In Pawn Duel pawns never promote, and en passant is not played.
Before you push a pawn, check whether an opposing pawn could capture it.

beats.label: A game of pawns
beats.say: Pawn Duel is a game played with pawns alone. It is a fun way to practise moving and capturing with pawns.
beats.speak: Pawn Duel is a game played with pawns alone. It is a fun way to practise moving and capturing with pawns.

beats.label: The starting position
beats.say: Each side has six pawns. White's stand from b2 to g2, and Black's stand from b7 to g7.
beats.speak: Each side has six pawns. White's stand from B two to G two, and Black's stand from B seven to G seven.

beats.label: White moves first
beats.say: White moves first, and the players take turns. Pawns move as usual, so White's pawn makes a double step from e2 to e4.
beats.speak: White moves first, and the players take turns. Pawns move as usual, so White's pawn makes a double step from E two to E four.

beats.label: Black replies
beats.say: Black answers with a double step too, from d7 to d5. Now the two pawns attack each other.
beats.speak: Black answers with a double step too, from D seven to D five. Now the two pawns attack each other.

beats.label: Capturing as usual
beats.say: Pawns capture diagonally, just as in a real game. White's pawn takes on d5, moving from e4 to d5.
beats.speak: Pawns capture diagonally, just as in a real game. White's pawn takes on D five, moving from E four to D five.

beats.label: Win by reaching the end
beats.say: The first way to win is to reach the far rank. This white pawn on c7 is one step from c8. If it gets there, White wins at once.
beats.speak: The first way to win is to reach the far rank. This white pawn on C seven is one step from C eight. If it gets there, White wins at once.

beats.label: Black reaches rank 1
beats.say: Black aims the other way. A black pawn that reaches the first rank wins the game, so this pawn on f2 needs just one more step.
beats.speak: Black aims the other way. A black pawn that reaches the first rank wins the game, so this pawn on F two needs just one more step.

beats.label: Win by capturing them all
beats.say: The second way is to capture every opposing pawn. White takes Black's last pawn, moving from d5 to e6. Every black pawn is now gone, and the game goes to White.
beats.speak: The second way is to capture every opposing pawn. White takes Black's last pawn, moving from D five to E six. Every black pawn is now gone, and the game goes to White.

beats.label: Win when they cannot move
beats.say: The third way: your opponent has no move on their turn. White's pawn steps from b4 to b5.
beats.speak: The third way: your opponent has no move on their turn. White's pawn steps from B four to B five.

beats.label: Black is stuck
beats.say: Now both black pawns are blocked, and nothing stands diagonally in front of them to capture. Black has no move, so White wins.
beats.speak: Now both black pawns are blocked, and nothing stands diagonally in front of them to capture. Black has no move, so White wins.

beats.label: No promotion, no en passant
beats.say: In Pawn Duel a pawn never turns into another piece, and one special pawn capture is left out. You will meet both in Promotion and En Passant.
beats.speak: In Pawn Duel a pawn never turns into another piece, and one special pawn capture is left out. You will meet both in Promotion and En Passant.

beats.label: Look before you push
beats.say: Look before you push. If this white pawn moves to e5, the black pawn on d6 can capture it.
beats.speak: Look before you push. If this white pawn moves to E five, the black pawn on D six can capture it.

beats.label: Guard your pawns
beats.say: A pawn guarded by another pawn is hard to win. If Black's pawn on e5 takes on d4, the pawn on c3 takes it back.
beats.speak: A pawn guarded by another pawn is hard to win. If Black's pawn on E five takes on D four, the pawn on C three takes it back.

beats.label: Count the race
beats.say: When two pawns race, count the steps. White's pawn on g4 needs four moves to reach g8, and Black's pawn on b6 needs five to reach b1.
beats.speak: When two pawns race, count the steps. White's pawn on G four needs four moves to reach G eight, and Black's pawn on B six needs five to reach B one.

beats.label: Play Pawn Duel
beats.say: Now play Pawn Duel yourself. Play against the computer, which takes Black, or share this device with a friend. You can also play it with real pawns on a real board.
beats.speak: Now play Pawn Duel yourself. Play against the computer, which takes Black, or share this device with a friend. You can also play it with real pawns on a real board.

lessons.title: The Rook
teaches: The rook moves in straight lines, along ranks and files, never diagonally.
It can travel any distance in one move, but only while the path is clear.
The rook cannot jump over pieces, its own or the enemy's.
It captures by landing on an enemy piece's square, which removes that piece.
A rook is worth five points.

beats.label: Meet the rook
beats.say: This tall piece with a notched top, like a castle tower, is the rook. Each player begins with two rooks in the corners, with the king between them: White's on a1 and h1, Black's on a8 and h8.
beats.speak: This tall piece with a notched top, like a castle tower, is the rook. Each player begins with two rooks in the corners, with the king between them: White's on A one and H one, Black's on A eight and H eight.

beats.label: Straight lines
beats.say: The rook moves in straight lines. It can go up or down its file, or sideways along its rank.
beats.speak: The rook moves in straight lines. It can go up or down its file, or sideways along its rank.

beats.label: Any distance
beats.say: It may travel as far as it likes in one move. Here the rook slides from c5 all the way along the rank to h5.
beats.speak: It may travel as far as it likes in one move. Here the rook slides from C five all the way along the rank to H five.

beats.label: Counting its squares
beats.say: Back on c5, let's count every square the rook could reach in one move. There are fourteen of them.
beats.speak: Back on C five, let's count every square the rook could reach in one move. There are fourteen of them.

beats.label: Fourteen from anywhere
beats.say: On an empty board, the rook reaches fourteen squares from any square at all, even from a corner like h8: seven down the file and seven along the rank.
beats.speak: On an empty board, the rook reaches fourteen squares from any square at all, even from a corner like H eight: seven down the file and seven along the rank.

beats.label: Never diagonally
beats.say: The rook never moves diagonally. The four squares touching c5 at the corners are out of its reach in one move.
beats.speak: The rook never moves diagonally. The four squares touching C five at the corners are out of its reach in one move.

beats.label: A clear path
beats.say: The rook cannot jump over anything. White's own pawn on d6 blocks the file, so d7 and d8 are out of reach.
beats.speak: The rook cannot jump over anything. White's own pawn on D six blocks the file, so D seven and D eight are out of reach.

beats.label: Blocked on the rank
beats.say: The pawn on f4 does the same along the rank. The rook can stop on e4, but g4 and h4 are behind the pawn.
beats.speak: The pawn on F four does the same along the rank. The rook can stop on E four, but G four and H four are behind the pawn.

beats.label: Not on its own pieces
beats.say: A rook can never land on a square held by its own side. To this rook, the white pawns are walls, not targets.
beats.speak: A rook can never land on a square held by its own side. To this rook, the white pawns are walls, not targets.

beats.label: Capturing
beats.say: The rook captures the same way it moves. Here it can reach Black's knight on d7 and Black's pawn on g4.
beats.speak: The rook captures the same way it moves. Here it can reach Black's knight on D seven and Black's pawn on G four.

beats.label: Taking the knight
beats.say: The rook moves from d4 to d7 and takes the knight's place. The captured knight leaves the board for good.
beats.speak: The rook moves from D four to D seven and takes the knight's place. The captured knight leaves the board for good.

beats.label: Only the first piece
beats.say: A rook can capture only the first enemy piece in its line. The rook on a1 can take the pawn on a5, but the queen on a8, behind that pawn, is out of reach.
beats.speak: A rook can capture only the first enemy piece in its line. The rook on A one can take the pawn on A five, but the queen on A eight, behind that pawn, is out of reach.

beats.label: Open lines
beats.say: Rooks love open lines. The rook on d1 sees all the way up the empty d-file, while the rook on a1 is blocked by its own pawn on a2 and can only shuffle along the first rank.
beats.speak: Rooks love open lines. The rook on D one sees all the way up the empty d-file, while the rook on A one is blocked by its own pawn on A two and can only shuffle along the first rank.

beats.label: Rooks protect each other
beats.say: Two rooks on the same rank or file, with nothing between them, guard each other. If one is captured, the other can take back.
beats.speak: Two rooks on the same rank or file, with nothing between them, guard each other. If one is captured, the other can take back.

beats.label: Worth five points
beats.say: A rook is worth five points, as much as five pawns. Of the pieces that are counted in points, only the queen is worth more.
beats.speak: A rook is worth five points, as much as five pawns. Of the pieces that are counted in points, only the queen is worth more.

beats.label: Look before you capture

beats.label: Summary

beats.label: Two rook games

beats.label: Rook Sweep

beats.label: Only the rooks move

beats.label: Black replies

beats.label: Guard your rook

beats.speak: The rooks can capture each other too, and a side that loses its rook loses the game. A side with no move on its turn also loses.

beats.label: A tempting pawn

beats.label: The trap

beats.speak: White's rook captures the pawn on D seven. Black's rook then captures White's rook from H seven, along the empty seventh rank, and Black wins.

beats.label: Check the lines

beats.label: Rooks and Pawns

beats.label: Everything moves

beats.label: Face to face

beats.label: Winning by capture

beats.label: Draws

lessons.title: The Bishop
teaches: The bishop moves along diagonals, any distance, while the path is clear.
Whatever colour of square a bishop begins on, it keeps for the whole game.
Each player has one light-squared bishop and one dark-squared bishop.
The bishop captures by landing on an enemy piece and cannot jump over pieces.
A bishop is worth three points.

beats.label: Meet the bishop
beats.say: Meet the bishop, the piece with a pointed, slanted top. Each player starts with two, either side of the queen and king: White's on c1 and f1, Black's on c8 and f8.
beats.speak: Meet the bishop, the piece with a pointed, slanted top. Each player starts with two, either side of the queen and king: White's on C one and F one, Black's on C eight and F eight.

beats.label: Diagonal lines
beats.say: The bishop moves along diagonals: slanting lines of squares that touch corner to corner. From e4 it has four directions to choose from.
beats.speak: The bishop moves along diagonals: slanting lines of squares that touch corner to corner. From E four it has four directions to choose from.

beats.label: Any distance
beats.say: Like the rook, it may travel as far as it likes in one move. Here the bishop glides from e4 to a8.
beats.speak: Like the rook, it may travel as far as it likes in one move. Here the bishop glides from E four to A eight.

beats.label: Counting its squares
beats.say: Back on e4, let's count the squares it could reach in one move. There are thirteen.
beats.speak: Back on E four, let's count the squares it could reach in one move. There are thirteen.

beats.label: Fewer from the corner
beats.say: Unlike the rook, the bishop reaches fewer squares from the edge. From the corner a1 it has a single diagonal, just seven squares long.
beats.speak: Unlike the rook, the bishop reaches fewer squares from the edge. From the corner A one it has a single diagonal, just seven squares long.

beats.label: One colour forever
beats.say: Look at the colours. The bishop on e4 stands on a light square, and every square it can reach is light too. A bishop never changes its square colour.
beats.speak: Look at the colours. The bishop on E four stands on a light square, and every square it can reach is light too. A bishop never changes its square colour.

beats.label: Light and dark
beats.say: So each player has one bishop for each colour. White's bishop on c1 stands on a dark square, and the one on f1 on a light square.
beats.speak: So each player has one bishop for each colour. White's bishop on C one stands on a dark square, and the one on F one on a light square.

beats.label: Black's bishops
beats.say: Black's bishops are the same pair the other way round: the bishop on c8 is on a light square, and the one on f8 is on a dark square.
beats.speak: Black's bishops are the same pair the other way round: the bishop on C eight is on a light square, and the one on F eight is on a dark square.

beats.label: No jumping
beats.say: The bishop cannot jump. Its own pawn on g6 stops it at f5, so h7 is out of reach.
beats.speak: The bishop cannot jump. Its own pawn on G six stops it at F five, so H seven is out of reach.

beats.label: Hemmed in at the start
beats.say: At the start of a game, the bishops are shut in by their own pawns. The pawns on b2 and d2 block both diagonals of the bishop on c1.
beats.speak: At the start of a game, the bishops are shut in by their own pawns. The pawns on B two and D two block both diagonals of the bishop on C one.

beats.label: Opening a diagonal
beats.say: Now White's pawn steps forward from d2 to d4, out of the bishop's way. The c1 bishop can now see along a clear line through d2, e3, f4, g5 and h6.
beats.speak: Now White's pawn steps forward from D two to D four, out of the bishop's way. The C one bishop can now see along a clear line through D two, E three, F four, G five and H six.

beats.label: Capturing
beats.say: The bishop captures the way it moves, by landing on an enemy piece. From c4 it can reach Black's knight on f7 and Black's pawn on a6.
beats.speak: The bishop captures the way it moves, by landing on an enemy piece. From C four it can reach Black's knight on F seven and Black's pawn on A six.

beats.label: Taking the knight
beats.say: The bishop moves from c4 to f7 and captures the knight, which leaves the board.
beats.speak: The bishop moves from C four to F seven and captures the knight, which leaves the board.

beats.label: Out of reach
beats.say: A bishop can only ever attack pieces on its own colour. Black's rook on e5 sits right beside this light-squared bishop, but e5 is dark, so the bishop can never touch it.
beats.speak: A bishop can only ever attack pieces on its own colour. Black's rook on E five sits right beside this light-squared bishop, but E five is dark, so the bishop can never touch it.

beats.label: Two bishops together
beats.say: A pair of bishops works as a team. One covers the light squares and the other covers the dark squares.
beats.speak: A pair of bishops works as a team. One covers the light squares and the other covers the dark squares.

beats.label: Worth three points
beats.say: A bishop is worth three points, as much as three pawns. A rook, worth five, is worth more than a bishop.
beats.speak: A bishop is worth three points, as much as three pawns. A rook, worth five, is worth more than a bishop.

beats.label: Mind the pawns
beats.say: Pawns are good at catching bishops. If White's bishop went from c1 to g5, Black's pawn on h6 could capture it. Check before you land.
beats.speak: Pawns are good at catching bishops. If White's bishop went from C one to G five, Black's pawn on H six could capture it. Check before you land.

beats.label: Summary
beats.say: The bishop moves diagonally, any distance, never through pieces. It stays on one colour all game, and it is worth three points.
beats.speak: The bishop moves diagonally, any distance, never through pieces. It stays on one colour all game, and it is worth three points.

beats.speak: White's bishop captures the pawn on B four. It is safe there: Black's dark-squared bishop on G seven stands on no diagonal through B four, and in this game pawns never capture.

beats.label: Safe from the other bishop

beats.speak: Bishops on different colours can never capture each other. Black's bishop on E six moves on light squares, so it can never reach White's bishop on B four.

beats.label: When nobody can win

beats.speak: White's bishop moves from D one to H five, aiming at the pawn on F seven. Black's pawn moves from G seven to G six. It blocks the bishop's line and attacks the bishop.

lessons.title: The Queen
teaches: The queen combines the rook's straight lines with the bishop's diagonals, sliding any distance along a clear path.
She moves in one straight direction per move and cannot jump over pieces.
She captures by landing on an enemy piece and taking its place.
Each queen starts on her own colour: White's on d1, Black's on d8.
The queen is worth nine points, so check that her new square is safe before you move her.

beats.label: Meet the queen
beats.say: This is the queen, the most powerful piece in chess. Each player has one.
beats.speak: This is the queen, the most powerful piece in chess. Each player has one.

beats.label: Straight lines like a rook
beats.say: Just as a rook does, she slides along ranks and files, up, down, left or right, any distance she wants.
beats.speak: Just as a rook does, she slides along ranks and files, up, down, left or right, any distance she wants.

beats.label: Diagonals like a bishop
beats.say: Like a bishop, she also moves along diagonals, as far as she likes.
beats.speak: Like a bishop, she also moves along diagonals, as far as she likes.

beats.label: Eight directions
beats.say: Put the two together and she has eight directions. On this empty board, the queen on f4 can reach twenty-five squares.
beats.speak: Put the two together and she has eight directions. On this empty board, the queen on F four can reach twenty-five squares.

beats.label: One direction per move
beats.say: In one move she picks a single direction and goes as far as she wants. Here she slides diagonally from f4 to c7.
beats.speak: In one move she picks a single direction and goes as far as she wants. Here she slides diagonally from F four to C seven.

beats.label: She cannot jump
beats.say: Like the rook and the bishop, the queen cannot jump. Her own pawn on d4 stops her: she can reach d2 and d3, but not d4 or beyond.
beats.speak: Like the rook and the bishop, the queen cannot jump. Her own pawn on D four stops her: she can reach D two and D three, but not D four or beyond.

beats.label: A target on her line
beats.say: Now a black knight stands on g7. The diagonal from the queen on b2 to g7 is clear, so the queen attacks it.
beats.speak: Now a black knight stands on G seven. The diagonal from the queen on B two to G seven is clear, so the queen attacks it.

beats.label: Capture by replacement
beats.say: The queen captures the way she moves. She goes from b2 to g7, the knight leaves the board, and she takes its place.
beats.speak: The queen captures the way she moves. She goes from B two to G seven, the knight leaves the board, and she takes its place.

beats.label: Where the queens start
beats.say: At the start of a game, White's queen stands on d1 and Black's queen on d8.
beats.speak: At the start of a game, White's queen stands on D one and Black's queen on D eight.

beats.label: Queen on her colour
beats.say: Each queen begins on a square of her own colour. White's queen begins on d1, a light square. Black's queen begins on d8, a dark square.
beats.speak: Each queen begins on a square of her own colour. White's queen begins on D one, a light square. Black's queen begins on D eight, a dark square.

beats.label: Worth nine points
beats.say: The queen is worth nine points. A rook and a bishop together are worth only eight.
beats.speak: The queen is worth nine points. A rook and a bishop together are worth only eight.

beats.label: Danger from small pieces
beats.say: Because she is worth so much, losing her hurts. Here the white queen on e5 stands where the black pawn on d6 can capture her.
beats.speak: Because she is worth so much, losing her hurts. Here the white queen on E five stands where the black pawn on D six can capture her.

beats.label: A costly loss
beats.say: Black's pawn captures from d6 to e5. Black gave up nothing and won nine points with a one-point pawn.
beats.speak: Black's pawn captures from D six to E five. Black gave up nothing and won nine points with a one-point pawn.

beats.label: Look before you move
beats.say: Before moving your queen, look at her new square. She could go from d1 to g4, but the black bishop on e6 attacks g4.
beats.speak: Before moving your queen, look at her new square. She could go from D one to G four, but the black bishop on E six attacks G four.

beats.label: Choose a safe square
beats.say: On a4 no black piece can reach her. That square is safe.
beats.speak: On A four no black piece can reach her. That square is safe.

beats.label: A safe move
beats.say: So the queen goes from d1 to a4, where she is safe.
beats.speak: So the queen goes from D one to A four, where she is safe.

beats.label: Many attacks at once
beats.say: Her long reach lets her attack in several directions at once. From d5 this queen attacks the rook on a8, the knight on d8 and the bishop on h5.
beats.speak: Her long reach lets her attack in several directions at once. From D five this queen attacks the rook on A eight, the knight on D eight and the bishop on H five.

beats.label: Remember
beats.say: To sum up: rook lines plus bishop lines, a home square of her own colour, and a value of nine points. Keep her safe.
beats.speak: To sum up: rook lines plus bishop lines, a home square of her own colour, and a value of nine points. Keep her safe.

beats.speak: With the pawns, keep them close together and protect as many as you can, and look for a pawn the queen cannot stop.

beats.speak: Now play Queen Against Pawns here against the computer, which plays the queen, or with a friend on this device. You can also set it up on a real board.

lessons.title: The Knight
teaches: A knight jumps in an L: two squares along a rank or file, then one square sideways.
The knight is the only piece that can jump over other pieces.
It captures only on the square where it lands.
Every knight move lands on a square of the other colour.
A knight in the centre reaches up to eight squares, but only a few from the edge or a corner.
A knight is worth three points.

beats.label: Meet the knight
beats.say: This is the knight. It looks like a horse's head, and it moves unlike any other piece.
beats.speak: This is the knight. It looks like a horse's head, and it moves unlike any other piece.

beats.label: The L shape
beats.say: Its move makes an L: two squares along a rank or file, then one square sideways. From f5, two squares up is f7, and one sideways is g7.
beats.speak: Its move makes an L: two squares along a rank or file, then one square sideways. From F five, two squares up is F seven, and one sideways is G seven.

beats.label: A knight move
beats.say: Here it goes. The knight lands on g7. It never stops on the squares in between.
beats.speak: Here it goes. The knight lands on G seven. It never stops on the squares in between.

beats.label: All its squares
beats.say: Back on f5, the knight has eight squares it can jump to. Let's count them.
beats.speak: Back on F five, the knight has eight squares it can jump to. Let's count them.

beats.label: It jumps
beats.say: In ordinary moves, the knight is the only piece that can jump over others. This knight on e3 is boxed in by pawns, yet it still has eight squares to go to.
beats.speak: In ordinary moves, the knight is the only piece that can jump over others. This knight on E three is boxed in by pawns, yet it still has eight squares to go to.

beats.label: Over the pawns
beats.say: The knight leaps from e3 to f5, straight over its own pawns.
beats.speak: The knight leaps from E three to F five, straight over its own pawns.

beats.label: Capturing
beats.say: The knight captures only where it lands. This knight on c3 attacks the rook on b5. It does not touch the pawns it jumps over.
beats.speak: The knight captures only where it lands. This knight on C three attacks the rook on B five. It does not touch the pawns it jumps over.

beats.label: Taking the rook
beats.say: White's knight jumps from c3 to b5 and captures the rook. The black pawns stay where they are.
beats.speak: White's knight jumps from C three to B five and captures the rook. The black pawns stay where they are.

beats.label: Changing colour
beats.say: Here is a neat fact. The knight on f5 stands on a light square, and every square it can reach is dark.
beats.speak: Here is a neat fact. The knight on F five stands on a light square, and every square it can reach is dark.

beats.label: Light to dark
beats.say: The knight jumps from f5 to d6, a dark square. From d6, every square it can reach is light.
beats.speak: The knight jumps from F five to D six, a dark square. From D six, every square it can reach is light.

beats.label: Edge squares
beats.say: Near the edge the knight has fewer choices. On a5 it can reach only four squares.
beats.speak: Near the edge the knight has fewer choices. On A five it can reach only four squares.

beats.label: Corner squares
beats.say: In a corner it is even worse. On h8 the knight has just two squares: f7 and g6.
beats.speak: In a corner it is even worse. On H eight the knight has just two squares: F seven and G six.

beats.label: Keep knights central
beats.say: So knights are usually happiest near the centre. The white knight on d5 reaches eight squares, while the black knight on h8 reaches only two.
beats.speak: So knights are usually happiest near the centre. The white knight on D five reaches eight squares, while the black knight on H eight reaches only two.

beats.label: Where knights start
beats.say: Each player has two knights. They start between the rooks and the bishops: White's on b1 and g1, Black's on b8 and g8.
beats.speak: Each player has two knights. They start between the rooks and the bishops: White's on B one and G one, Black's on B eight and G eight.

beats.label: Out over the pawns
beats.say: Because it jumps, a knight can leave home before any pawn moves. Right from the start, each white knight can already jump to two squares.
beats.speak: Because it jumps, a knight can leave home before any pawn moves. Right from the start, each white knight can already jump to two squares.

beats.label: Hard to see
beats.say: Knight attacks are easy to miss, because they do not follow a line. This black knight on e3 attacks both the queen on d1 and the rook on f1.
beats.speak: Knight attacks are easy to miss, because they do not follow a line. This black knight on E three attacks both the queen on D one and the rook on F one.

beats.label: Worth three points
beats.say: A knight is worth three points, the same as a bishop.
beats.speak: A knight is worth three points, the same as a bishop.

beats.label: Remember
beats.say: Remember: two squares straight, then one to the side. The knight jumps, changes colour every move, and likes the centre.
beats.speak: Remember: two squares straight, then one to the side. The knight jumps, changes colour every move, and likes the centre.

lessons.title: Knight Practice
teaches: In Knight Capture only the knights move; every other piece is a target that stays still.
Take every enemy piece and you win; if your knight is captured or cannot move on your turn, you lose.
Before jumping, check that the enemy knight cannot capture you on your new square.
In Knight Corners, visit a8, h8 and h1, then return to a1, never landing on a pawn or a square a pawn attacks.
Each trip between corners can be done in five moves.

beats.label: Two knight games
beats.say: Here are two games to sharpen your knight jumps. The first is Knight Capture.
beats.speak: Here are two games to sharpen your knight jumps. The first is Knight Capture.

beats.label: The layout
beats.say: Each side has a knight, a bishop, a rook and five pawns. White's knight starts on b1, and Black's on g8.
beats.speak: Each side has a knight, a bishop, a rook and five pawns. White's knight starts on B one, and Black's on G eight.

beats.label: Only knights move
beats.say: Only the knights move. The bishops, rooks and pawns never move: they are targets waiting to be captured.
beats.speak: Only the knights move. The bishops, rooks and pawns never move: they are targets waiting to be captured.

beats.label: First moves
beats.say: White moves first. White's knight jumps from b1 to c3. Black's knight jumps from g8 to f6.
beats.speak: White moves first. White's knight jumps from B one to C three. Black's knight jumps from G eight to F six.

beats.label: A tempting jump
beats.say: Suppose White's knight jumps from c3 to d5. From there it attacks the black bishop on e7.
beats.speak: Suppose White's knight jumps from C three to D five. From there it attacks the black bishop on E seven.

beats.label: Spot the danger
beats.say: But the black knight on f6 attacks d5 as well. The white knight has jumped into danger.
beats.speak: But the black knight on F six attacks D five as well. The white knight has jumped into danger.

beats.label: Losing the knight
beats.say: Black's knight captures from f6 to d5. White has lost the knight, and losing your knight loses the game.
beats.speak: Black's knight captures from F six to D five. White has lost the knight, and losing your knight loses the game.

beats.label: A safer jump
beats.say: Let's try again. This time White's knight jumps from c3 to b5, where the black knight cannot reach it. It attacks the pawn on d6.
beats.speak: Let's try again. This time White's knight jumps from C three to B five, where the black knight cannot reach it. It attacks the pawn on D six.

beats.label: A safe capture
beats.say: Black's knight jumps from f6 to h5. White's knight captures the pawn, jumping from b5 to d6.
beats.speak: Black's knight jumps from F six to H five. White's knight captures the pawn, jumping from B five to D six.

beats.label: New targets
beats.say: From d6 the white knight now attacks the rook on c8 and the pawns on b7 and f5.
beats.speak: From D six the white knight now attacks the rook on C eight and the pawns on B seven and F five.

beats.label: How to win
beats.say: Whoever captures every opposing piece wins. A player whose knight is taken, or whose knight cannot move on their turn, loses.
beats.speak: Whoever captures every opposing piece wins. A player whose knight is taken, or whose knight cannot move on their turn, loses.

beats.label: Knight Corners
beats.say: The second game, Knight Corners, you play alone. Your white knight starts on a1, and six black pawns stand still around the board.
beats.speak: The second game, Knight Corners, you play alone. Your white knight starts on A one, and six black pawns stand still around the board.

beats.label: The journey
beats.say: Your task is to visit a8, then h8, then h1, and finally come back home to a1.
beats.speak: Your task is to visit A eight, then H eight, then H one, and finally come back home to A one.

beats.label: Forbidden squares
beats.say: The knight must not land on a pawn, nor on any square a pawn guards. Black pawns guard the two squares diagonally ahead of them, towards rank 1.
beats.speak: The knight must not land on a pawn, nor on any square a pawn guards. Black pawns guard the two squares diagonally ahead of them, towards rank 1.

beats.label: Five moves each
beats.say: Each trip from one corner to the next takes at least five moves. Try to make every trip in five.
beats.speak: Each trip from one corner to the next takes at least five moves. Try to make every trip in five.

beats.label: A first jump
beats.say: From a1 the knight can go to b3 or c2, and both are safe. Here it jumps from a1 to c2.
beats.speak: From A one the knight can go to B three or C two, and both are safe. Here it jumps from A one to C two.

beats.label: Your turn to play
beats.say: Now play Knight Capture here against the computer, which plays Black, or with a friend on this device, and try Knight Corners on your own. Both work on a real board too.
beats.speak: Now play Knight Capture here against the computer, which plays Black, or with a friend on this device, and try Knight Corners on your own. Both work on a real board too.

lessons.title: The King
teaches: The king moves one square at a time, in any direction.
A king may never move onto a square the opponent attacks.
The two kings can never stand on neighbouring squares.
The king has no point value: it is never traded or captured.
A king that is attacked is in check, and the danger must be dealt with at once.

beats.label: Meet the king
beats.say: Meet the king, the most important piece on the board. Each side has exactly one, and the whole game is about keeping yours safe.
beats.speak: Meet the king, the most important piece on the board. Each side has exactly one, and the whole game is about keeping yours safe.

beats.label: Where the kings start
beats.say: White's king starts on e1 and Black's king starts on e8, each right beside its own queen.
beats.speak: White's king starts on E one and Black's king starts on E eight, each right beside its own queen.

beats.label: One step in any direction
beats.say: The king moves just one square at a time, but in any direction: forwards, backwards, sideways or diagonally.
beats.speak: The king moves just one square at a time, but in any direction: forwards, backwards, sideways or diagonally.

beats.label: Eight squares from the middle
beats.say: From d5, in the middle of the board, that gives the king eight squares to choose from.
beats.speak: From D five, in the middle of the board, that gives the king eight squares to choose from.

beats.label: A single step
beats.say: Here the king steps diagonally from d5 to e6. It moves one square per turn; the only exception is castling, a special move you will meet later.
beats.speak: Here the king steps diagonally from D five to E six. It moves one square per turn; the only exception is castling, a special move you will meet later.

beats.label: Fewer squares in a corner
beats.say: In a corner the king has far less room. From a1 it can reach only a2, b1 and b2.
beats.speak: In a corner the king has far less room. From A one it can reach only A two, B one and B two.

beats.label: Capturing with the king
beats.say: The king captures the same way it moves. The black knight on f5 stands next to it with nothing protecting it, so the king takes it by stepping from e4 to f5.
beats.speak: The king captures the same way it moves. The black knight on F five stands next to it with nothing protecting it, so the king takes it by stepping from E four to F five.

beats.label: Never into attack
beats.say: A king may never move onto a square that an enemy piece attacks. The rook on h5 attacks the whole fifth rank, so d5, e5 and f5 are forbidden.
beats.speak: A king may never move onto a square that an enemy piece attacks. The rook on H five attacks the whole fifth rank, so D five, E five and F five are forbidden.

beats.label: Five safe squares left
beats.say: The king still has five safe squares to choose from: d3, e3, f3, d4 and f4.
beats.speak: The king still has five safe squares to choose from: D three, E three, F three, D four and F four.

beats.label: No capturing protected pieces
beats.say: The king cannot capture a protected piece either. The pawn on f6 guards the knight on e5, so taking it would put the king straight into attack.
beats.speak: The king cannot capture a protected piece either. The pawn on F six guards the knight on E five, so taking it would put the king straight into attack.

beats.label: An attacked king is in check
beats.say: When a king is attacked, we say it is in check. The rook on e8 attacks straight down the e-file to the white king on e3.
beats.speak: When a king is attacked, we say it is in check. The rook on E eight attacks straight down the e-file to the white king on E three.

beats.label: Getting out of check
beats.say: A king in check must be rescued at once. Here the king steps sideways from e3 to d3, off the rook's file, and is safe again.
beats.speak: A king in check must be rescued at once. Here the king steps sideways from E three to D three, off the rook's file, and is safe again.

beats.label: More ways out later
beats.say: Stepping aside is one way out of check. You will meet all the ways out, and the end of the game, in Check and Checkmate.
beats.speak: Stepping aside is one way out of check. You will meet all the ways out, and the end of the game, in Check and Checkmate.

beats.label: Kings keep apart
beats.say: Two kings can never stand side by side. The squares b5, c5 and d5 touch both kings, so neither king may step onto any of them.
beats.speak: Two kings can never stand side by side. The squares B five, C five and D five touch both kings, so neither king may step onto any of them.

beats.label: Why kings keep apart
beats.say: Each king attacks every square around it. Stepping next to the other king would mean moving into attack, so there is always at least one square between them.
beats.speak: Each king attacks every square around it. Stepping next to the other king would mean moving into attack, so there is always at least one square between them.

beats.label: Worth the whole game
beats.say: Pawns, knights, bishops, rooks and queens all have point values. The king has none, because it is never traded or captured: if it is trapped in check with no escape, the game is lost.
beats.speak: Pawns, knights, bishops, rooks and queens all have point values. The king has none, because it is never traded or captured: if it is trapped in check with no escape, the game is lost.

beats.label: A fighter in the endgame
beats.say: When only a few pieces are left, the king becomes a useful fighter. Here the white king steps from e2 to e3, right beside its pawn on d4, to protect it.
beats.speak: When only a few pieces are left, the king becomes a useful fighter. Here the white king steps from E two to E three, right beside its pawn on D four, to protect it.

beats.label: Remember
beats.say: A king steps one square at a time, whichever way it likes, but never into attack and never beside the other king. Keep it safe, and remember: an attacked king is in check.
beats.speak: A king steps one square at a time, whichever way it likes, but never into attack and never beside the other king. Keep it safe, and remember: an attacked king is in check.

lessons.title: Safe Squares
teaches: A square is attacked when an enemy piece could reach it by its normal movement.
Pawns attack the two squares diagonally in front of them, not the square straight ahead.
A line stops at the first piece in the way, but a king in check cannot escape by stepping away from the checker along its line.
The king cannot capture an enemy piece that another enemy piece protects.
Before a king walk, mark every attacked square and plan a route over the safe ones.

beats.label: Where may the king go?
beats.say: The king may only step onto safe squares. In this lesson you will learn to spot the dangerous ones, and then plan a walk around them.
beats.speak: The king may only step onto safe squares. In this lesson you will learn to spot the dangerous ones, and then plan a walk around them.

beats.label: What attacked means
beats.say: An enemy piece attacks every square it could reach by its normal movement, even if it may not actually move there this turn. This rook on c3 attacks every square along the c-file and the third rank.
beats.speak: An enemy piece attacks every square it could reach by its normal movement, even if it may not actually move there this turn. This rook on C three attacks every square along the c-file and the third rank.

beats.label: Bishops attack diagonals
beats.say: A bishop attacks along its diagonals. From f5, this one attacks eleven squares.
beats.speak: A bishop attacks along its diagonals. From F five, this one attacks eleven squares.

beats.label: Knights attack by jumping
beats.say: A knight attacks the squares it could jump to, whatever stands in between. The knight on d5 attacks eight squares.
beats.speak: A knight attacks the squares it could jump to, whatever stands in between. The knight on D five attacks eight squares.

beats.label: Pawns attack diagonally
beats.say: Pawns are the odd ones out. A pawn attacks only the two squares on its forward diagonals, never the square right in front of it. This black pawn on d5 attacks c4 and e4, while d4 is safe.
beats.speak: Pawns are the odd ones out. A pawn attacks only the two squares on its forward diagonals, never the square right in front of it. This black pawn on D five attacks C four and E four, while D four is safe.

beats.label: The enemy king attacks too
beats.say: The enemy king attacks every square around it. That is why your king can never step next to it.
beats.speak: The enemy king attacks every square around it. That is why your king can never step next to it.

beats.label: Pieces block lines
beats.say: A rook, bishop or queen attacks only until its line meets a piece. Along the fourth rank, the rook on a4 reaches b4, c4 and the pawn on d4, but not the squares beyond it.
beats.speak: A rook, bishop or queen attacks only until its line meets a piece. Along the fourth rank, the rook on A four reaches B four, C four and the pawn on D four, but not the squares beyond it.

beats.label: No stepping back along the line
beats.say: A king in check cannot escape by stepping away along the checking line. If the king left d4 for e4, d4 would no longer block the rook, so e4 would be attacked too. Both c4 and e4 are unsafe.
beats.speak: A king in check cannot escape by stepping away along the checking line. If the king left D four for E four, D four would no longer block the rook, so E four would be attacked too. Both C four and E four are unsafe.

beats.label: Protected pieces are off limits
beats.say: An enemy piece is only safe to capture if nothing protects it. The bishop on h6 guards the knight on f4, so f4 is not a safe square for the king.
beats.speak: An enemy piece is only safe to capture if nothing protects it. The bishop on H six guards the knight on F four, so F four is not a safe square for the king.

beats.label: Planning a king walk
beats.say: Now let's plan a walk. The white king on d2 wants to reach f6, but Black's rook and knight guard many squares on the way.
beats.speak: Now let's plan a walk. The white king on D two wants to reach F six, but Black's rook and knight guard many squares on the way.

beats.label: Mark the danger
beats.say: First, mark every empty square the black pieces attack. The rook covers the fifth rank and the d-file above the pawn, the knight covers squares such as e4, f3 and h3, and the black king guards the squares around it.
beats.speak: First, mark every empty square the black pieces attack. The rook covers the fifth rank and the d-file above the pawn, the knight covers squares such as E four, F three and H three, and the black king guards the squares around it.

beats.label: The pawn as a shield
beats.say: The white pawn on d3 blocks the rook's file. That is why d2, where the king stands, is safe.
beats.speak: The white pawn on D three blocks the rook's file. That is why D two, where the king stands, is safe.

beats.label: Find the gap
beats.say: Now look along the fifth rank. The rook protects the knight on g5, so the king cannot take it. The only empty safe square on that rank is h5.
beats.speak: Now look along the fifth rank. The rook protects the knight on G five, so the king cannot take it. The only empty safe square on that rank is H five.

beats.label: The route
beats.say: So the route bends: e3, f4 and g4, then through the gap at h5, and back across to g6 and f6. Every one of those squares is safe.
beats.speak: So the route bends: E three, F four and G four, then through the gap at H five, and back across to G six and F six. Every one of those squares is safe.

beats.label: Walking, part one
beats.say: The king steps from d2 to e3. Then it steps from e3 to f4. Then it steps from f4 to g4.
beats.speak: The king steps from D two to E three. Then it steps from E three to F four. Then it steps from F four to G four.

beats.label: Walking, part two
beats.say: Next the king slips from g4 to h5. Then it steps from h5 to g6. Finally it steps from g6 to f6 and has arrived.
beats.speak: Next the king slips from G four to H five. Then it steps from H five to G six. Finally it steps from G six to F six and has arrived.

beats.label: Look again each move
beats.say: In a real game Black moves too, so the safe squares keep changing. Look at the board again before every step.
beats.speak: In a real game Black moves too, so the safe squares keep changing. Look at the board again before every step.

beats.label: Remember
beats.say: Before the king moves, ask which squares are attacked. Step only on safe squares, and plan the whole route before you set off.
beats.speak: Before the king moves, ask which squares are attacked. Step only on safe squares, and plan the whole route before you set off.

lessons.title: Check and Checkmate
teaches: Check means the king is attacked, and it must be answered on the very next move.
Check can be answered in three ways: step the king to safety, put a piece in the way, or take the attacker.
A knight's check cannot be blocked, because knights jump.
Checkmate is a check with no way out, and it ends the game at once.

beats.label: The goal of chess
beats.say: The aim of chess is checkmate. To understand it, we first need a closer look at check.
beats.speak: The aim of chess is checkmate. To understand it, we first need a closer look at check.

beats.label: Check
beats.say: Check means the king is attacked. The black rook on e7 attacks the white king on e1, so White is in check.
beats.speak: Check means the king is attacked. The black rook on E seven attacks the white king on E one, so White is in check.

beats.label: Check must be answered
beats.say: A side in check must get out of it on the very next move. You may never make a move that leaves your own king attacked.
beats.speak: A side in check must get out of it on the very next move. You may never make a move that leaves your own king attacked.

beats.label: Three ways out
beats.say: You can answer a check in three ways. Step the king to safety, put a piece in the way, or take the attacker.
beats.speak: You can answer a check in three ways. Step the king to safety, put a piece in the way, or take the attacker.

beats.label: Way one: move the king
beats.say: First way: move the king to a safe square. From e1 it can go to d1, d2, f1 or f2, but not to e2, which is still on the rook's file.
beats.speak: First way: move the king to a safe square. From E one it can go to D one, D two, F one or F two, but not to E two, which is still on the rook's file.

beats.label: The king steps aside
beats.say: The king steps from e1 to d2. Nothing attacks it there, so the check is over.
beats.speak: The king steps from E one to D two. Nothing attacks it there, so the check is over.

beats.label: Way two: block
beats.say: Second way: put a piece in between. The rook on a1 checks the king on g1, and the king has no safe square to go to.
beats.speak: Second way: put a piece in between. The rook on A one checks the king on G one, and the king has no safe square to go to.

beats.label: The bishop blocks
beats.say: The bishop steps from e2 to f1, between the rook and the king. The rook's line now stops at the bishop, so the check is blocked.
beats.speak: The bishop steps from E two to F one, between the rook and the king. The rook's line now stops at the bishop, so the check is blocked.

beats.label: Way three: capture
beats.say: Third way: capture the piece giving check. The knight on d3 checks the king on e1, and a knight's check can never be blocked, because knights jump.
beats.speak: Third way: capture the piece giving check. The knight on D three checks the king on E one, and a knight's check can never be blocked, because knights jump.

beats.label: The pawn captures
beats.say: The pawn on c2 captures the knight on d3, and the check is over.
beats.speak: The pawn on C two captures the knight on D three, and the check is over.

beats.label: Checkmate
beats.say: Checkmate is a check with no way out: the king cannot escape, nothing can block, and nothing can capture the checking piece. The game ends at once.
beats.speak: Checkmate is a check with no way out: the king cannot escape, nothing can block, and nothing can capture the checking piece. The game ends at once.

beats.label: The rook gives check
beats.say: Black's rook swoops down from a8 to a1. Now the white king on g1 is in check.
beats.speak: Black's rook swoops down from A eight to A one. Now the white king on G one is in check.

beats.label: No way out
beats.say: The king cannot step to f1 or h1, which the rook attacks, and its own pawns fill f2, g2 and h2. No white piece can block or capture. Checkmate: Black wins.
beats.speak: The king cannot step to F one or H one, which the rook attacks, and its own pawns fill F two, G two and H two. No white piece can block or capture. Checkmate: Black wins.

beats.label: Queen and king together
beats.say: The queen and king make a strong team. The queen slides from h7 to e7, right in front of the black king, and the white king on e6 protects her.
beats.speak: The queen and king make a strong team. The queen slides from H seven to E seven, right in front of the black king, and the white king on E six protects her.

beats.label: Why it is checkmate
beats.say: The queen attacks d8, f8, d7 and f7. The black king cannot capture her either, because the white king guards her. Checkmate.
beats.speak: The queen attacks D eight, F eight, D seven and F seven. The black king cannot capture her either, because the white king guards her. Checkmate.

beats.label: A rook on the edge
beats.say: A rook can checkmate a king that is stuck on the edge. The white rook rushes up from h1 to h8, giving check along the eighth rank.
beats.speak: A rook can checkmate a king that is stuck on the edge. The white rook rushes up from H one to H eight, giving check along the eighth rank.

beats.label: Boxed in
beats.say: The rook's line covers b8 and d8, and the white king on c6 guards b7, c7 and d7. The black king has nowhere to go, so this is checkmate.
beats.speak: The rook's line covers B eight and D eight, and the white king on C six guards B seven, C seven and D seven. The black king has nowhere to go, so this is checkmate.

beats.label: Check, but not mate
beats.say: Compare this board, with the white king on c5. The same rook move to h8 gives check, but now the black king can step out to b7, c7 or d7.
beats.speak: Compare this board, with the white king on C five. The same rook move to H eight gives check, but now the black king can step out to B seven, C seven or D seven.

beats.label: Remember
beats.say: Check: the king is attacked, so answer it by moving, blocking or capturing. Checkmate: a check with no answer, and the game is over.
beats.speak: Check: the king is attacked, so answer it by moving, blocking or capturing. Checkmate: a check with no answer, and the game is over.

lessons.title: Setting Up the Board
teaches: Turn the board so the right-hand corner square nearest each player is light.
From each corner inwards come a rook, a knight and a bishop.
The queen goes on her own colour: White's on d1, Black's on d8.
The king stands beside his queen, on e1 for White and e8 for Black.
White's pawns stand on the second rank and Black's on the seventh, in front of the other pieces.

beats.label: Ready to set up
beats.say: Every game starts from the same position. Let's set up the board together, beginning with White's pieces.
beats.speak: Every game starts from the same position. Let's set up the board together, beginning with White's pieces.

beats.label: Light square bottom right
beats.say: First, turn the board so each player has a light square in the right-hand corner nearest to them. For White that square is h1; for Black it is a8.
beats.speak: First, turn the board so each player has a light square in the right-hand corner nearest to them. For White that square is H one; for Black it is A eight.

beats.label: Rooks in the corners
beats.say: White's two rooks go in White's corners, on a1 and h1.
beats.speak: White's two rooks go in White's corners, on A one and H one.

beats.label: Knights next
beats.say: Next to each rook goes a knight, so White's knights stand on b1 and g1.
beats.speak: Next to each rook goes a knight, so White's knights stand on B one and G one.

beats.label: Then the bishops
beats.say: Beside each knight goes a bishop. White's bishops stand on c1 and f1.
beats.speak: Beside each knight goes a bishop. White's bishops stand on C one and F one.

beats.label: Two squares left
beats.say: Two squares are still empty in the middle of White's back row: d1 and e1.
beats.speak: Two squares are still empty in the middle of White's back row: D one and E one.

beats.label: Queen on her colour
beats.say: The queen goes on the square of her own colour. White's queen is light, so she stands on d1, which is a light square.
beats.speak: The queen goes on the square of her own colour. White's queen is light, so she stands on D one, which is a light square.

beats.label: King beside her
beats.say: The king takes the last square, right beside his queen. White's king stands on e1.
beats.speak: The king takes the last square, right beside his queen. White's king stands on E one.

beats.label: White's back row
beats.say: From a1 to h1, White's back row now holds a rook, a knight, a bishop, the queen, the king, a bishop, a knight and a rook.
beats.speak: From A one to H one, White's back row now holds a rook, a knight, a bishop, the queen, the king, a bishop, a knight and a rook.

beats.label: Black mirrors White
beats.say: Black's back row mirrors White's. Black's rooks stand on a8 and h8, the knights on b8 and g8, and the bishops on c8 and f8.
beats.speak: Black's back row mirrors White's. Black's rooks stand on A eight and H eight, the knights on B eight and G eight, and the bishops on C eight and F eight.

beats.label: Black's queen
beats.say: Black's queen is dark, so she goes on the dark square d8. Now the two queens face each other along the d-file.
beats.speak: Black's queen is dark, so she goes on the dark square D eight. Now the two queens face each other along the d-file.

beats.label: Black's king and pawns
beats.say: Black's king goes beside his queen on e8. In front of them, Black's eight pawns fill the seventh rank.
beats.speak: Black's king goes beside his queen on E eight. In front of them, Black's eight pawns fill the seventh rank.

beats.label: White's pawns
beats.say: Last of all, White's eight pawns fill the second rank. The board is ready.
beats.speak: Last of all, White's eight pawns fill the second rank. The board is ready.

beats.label: A mirror image
beats.say: Each piece faces the same kind of piece along its file. Rook faces rook, queen faces queen, and king faces king.
beats.speak: Each piece faces the same kind of piece along its file. Rook faces rook, queen faces queen, and king faces king.

beats.label: Check your setup
beats.say: Before you play, check two things. Is the corner square on each player's right light? Is each queen on a square of her own colour?
beats.speak: Before you play, check two things. Is the corner square on each player's right light? Is each queen on a square of her own colour?

beats.label: Mistake: king and queen
beats.say: A common mistake is to swap the king and queen. Here the white queen stands on e1, a dark square, so this setup is wrong.
beats.speak: A common mistake is to swap the king and queen. Here the white queen stands on E one, a dark square, so this setup is wrong.

beats.label: Put it right
beats.say: Swap them back. Now the white queen is on d1, her own light square, with the king beside her on e1.
beats.speak: Swap them back. Now the white queen is on D one, her own light square, with the king beside her on E one.

beats.label: Mistake: knight and bishop
beats.say: Another slip is mixing up the knights and bishops. Here White's bishops stand on b1 and g1, next to the rooks, which is wrong.
beats.speak: Another slip is mixing up the knights and bishops. Here White's bishops stand on B one and G one, next to the rooks, which is wrong.

beats.label: Rook, knight, bishop
beats.say: Remember the order from each corner: rook, knight, bishop. With the knights on b1 and g1 and the bishops on c1 and f1, White's side is right again.
beats.speak: Remember the order from each corner: rook, knight, bishop. With the knights on B one and G one and the bishops on C one and F one, White's side is right again.

beats.label: Ready to play
beats.say: Every piece is in place. White moves first, so once the board is set, White begins.
beats.speak: Every piece is in place. White moves first, so once the board is set, White begins.

lessons.title: Castling
teaches: In castling the king slides two squares towards a rook, which then hops over and lands on the king's far side.
You can castle on the kingside (king to g1 or g8) or on the queenside (king to c1 or c8).
Castling tucks the king behind its pawns, away from the open centre.
Castling also brings a rook out of its corner, towards the centre.
On a real board, move the king first, then the rook, using one hand.

practice.goal: Castle kingside to make your king safe, then keep bringing out your pieces.
hints: Castling moves your king and a rook in one turn. Check which side has an empty path between the king and its rook.
Your knight and bishop have already left g1 and f1, but your bishop and queen still stand on c1 and d1.
practice.offTrack: That move is not castling. Undo it, then move your king two squares towards the rook on the side with a clear path; the rook hops over it.

mistakes.e1c1: You cannot castle queenside yet: your bishop on c1 and queen on d1 still stand between the king and the rook on a1.
mistakes.e1f1: That moves the king only one square, and a king that has moved can never castle. Undo it and move the king two squares instead.
mistakes.h1f1: Moving the rook first is not castling, and a rook that has moved can never castle. Undo it and start with your king.

practice.success: Well done: your king is tucked away on g1 behind its pawns, and your rook has come to f1, towards the centre. Keep bringing out your pieces.

beats.label: A special move
beats.say: Castling is a special move made by the king and a rook together. It is the only move in chess where you move two of your pieces at once.
beats.speak: Castling is a special move made by the king and a rook together. It is the only move in chess where you move two of your pieces at once.

beats.label: Castling on the kingside
beats.say: To castle on the kingside, the king moves two squares towards the h1 rook, from e1 to g1. Then the rook jumps over the king, from h1 to f1.
beats.speak: To castle on the kingside, the king moves two squares towards the H one rook, from E one to G one. Then the rook jumps over the king, from H one to F one.

beats.label: King and rook side by side
beats.say: Now the king stands on g1, near the corner, and the rook stands right beside it on f1.
beats.speak: Now the king stands on G one, near the corner, and the rook stands right beside it on F one.

beats.label: Castling on the queenside
