beats.say: Queenside castling works the same way. The king moves two squares towards the a1 rook, from e1 to c1. Then the rook jumps over the king, from a1 to d1.
beats.speak: Queenside castling works the same way. The king moves two squares towards the A one rook, from E one to C one. Then the rook jumps over the king, from A one to D one.

beats.label: The pattern
beats.say: Either way, the king always moves exactly two squares, and the rook lands right next to the king, on its other side.
beats.speak: Either way, the king always moves exactly two squares, and the rook lands right next to the king, on its other side.

beats.label: Black castles kingside
beats.say: Black castles in the same way. The king moves from e8 to g8. Then the rook jumps from h8 to f8.
beats.speak: Black castles in the same way. The king moves from E eight to G eight. Then the rook jumps from H eight to F eight.

beats.label: Black castles queenside
beats.say: Now Black castles on the queenside. The king travels from e8 to c8. Then the rook hops from a8 to d8.
beats.speak: Now Black castles on the queenside. The king travels from E eight to C eight. Then the rook hops from A eight to D eight.

beats.label: Short and long
beats.say: Kingside castling is often called short castling, and queenside castling long castling, because the queenside rook travels further.
beats.speak: Kingside castling is often called short castling, and queenside castling long castling, because the queenside rook travels further.

beats.label: Why castle? Danger in the centre
beats.say: Why castle? A king in the middle is in danger once pawns leave the centre. Here the d-file is open, with no pawns on it, and the black rook on d8 controls it, right beside the white king.
beats.speak: Why castle? A king in the middle is in danger once pawns leave the centre. Here the d-file is open, with no pawns on it, and the black rook on D eight controls it, right beside the white king.

beats.label: Safety behind the pawns
beats.say: So White castles. First the king slides across from e1 to g1. Then the rook hops over it from h1 to f1. Now the king sits behind the pawns on f2, g2 and h2, away from the open files.
beats.speak: So White castles. First the king slides across from E one to G one. Then the rook hops over it from H one to F one. Now the king sits behind the pawns on F two, G two and H two, away from the open files.

beats.label: The rook joins the game
beats.say: Castling also brings the rook towards the centre quickly. From f1 it can move straight to the open e-file or d-file.
beats.speak: Castling also brings the rook towards the centre quickly. From F one it can move straight to the open e-file or d-file.

beats.label: Queenside: rook to the centre
beats.say: Queenside castling brings the rook to the centre at once. First the king slides across from e1 to c1. Then the rook hops over it from a1 to d1, onto a central file.
beats.speak: Queenside castling brings the rook to the centre at once. First the king slides across from E one to C one. Then the rook hops over it from A one to D one, onto a central file.

beats.label: Clear the way first
beats.say: Castling needs a clear road between king and rook. Here the knight and bishop have already come out, so f1 and g1 are free.
beats.speak: Castling needs a clear road between king and rook. Here the knight and bishop have already come out, so F one and G one are free.

beats.label: Castle early
beats.say: Castling early, once your knight and bishop have moved out, is a good habit. The exact conditions come in Castling Rules.
beats.speak: Castling early, once your knight and bishop have moved out, is a good habit. The exact conditions come in Castling Rules.

beats.label: On a real board
beats.say: On a real board, move the king two squares first, then lift the rook over it, using the same hand. Moving the king first shows clearly that you are castling.
beats.speak: On a real board, move the king two squares first, then lift the rook over it, using the same hand. Moving the king first shows clearly that you are castling.

beats.label: Your turn
beats.say: Now try it yourself. In this position, castle to tuck your king behind its pawns and bring your rook towards the centre.
beats.speak: Now try it yourself. In this position, castle to tuck your king behind its pawns and bring your rook towards the centre.

lessons.title: Castling Rules
teaches: Nothing may stand between the king and the rook you castle with.
You can never castle if the king has moved, or with a rook that has moved.
You cannot castle out of check, through an attacked square, or into check.
In queenside castling the rook may pass over an attacked b1 or b8; only the king's squares must be safe.
A blocked path or an attack can change later, but a king or rook that has moved has lost its castling for good.

practice.goal: Work out which side you may castle on, castle there, then keep bringing out your pieces.
hints: Go through the checklist for each side: is the path empty, have the king and rook stayed at home, and is the king safe now, on the way and where it lands?
Follow the diagonal from Black's bishop on a6 towards your kingside. Which square that your king would cross does it attack?
practice.offTrack: That move is not castling. Undo it, then castle on the side where your king does not cross or land on an attacked square.

mistakes.e1g1: You cannot castle kingside here: Black's bishop on a6 attacks f1, the square your king would cross. Check the other side.
mistakes.e1d1: That moves the king only one square, and a king that has moved can never castle. Undo it and castle instead.

practice.success: Well done: you castled queenside, the only side allowed here, because Black's bishop on a6 attacks f1. Your king is on c1 and your rook on d1. Play on.

beats.label: Rules for a special move
beats.say: Castling is a powerful move, so it comes with strict rules. Check every one of them before you castle.
beats.speak: Castling is a powerful move, so it comes with strict rules. Check every one of them before you castle.

beats.label: Rule one: an empty path
beats.say: First, nothing may stand between the king and the rook. The bishop on f1 and the knight on g1 are in the way, so White cannot castle on the kingside yet.
beats.speak: First, nothing may stand between the king and the rook. The bishop on F one and the knight on G one are in the way, so White cannot castle on the kingside yet.

beats.label: Clearing the way
beats.say: The knight leaps out from g1 to f3. Then the bishop heads off from f1 to c4. Now f1 and g1 are both empty, and the path is clear.
beats.speak: The knight leaps out from G one to F three. Then the bishop heads off from F one to C four. Now F one and G one are both empty, and the path is clear.

beats.label: Three squares on the queenside
beats.say: On the queenside, three squares must be empty: b1, c1 and d1. Here the knight on b1 is still in the way, so queenside castling must wait.
beats.speak: On the queenside, three squares must be empty: B one, C one and D one. Here the knight on B one is still in the way, so queenside castling must wait.

beats.label: Rule two: the king has not moved
beats.say: Second, the king must never have moved. Here the king steps from e1 to f1. Later it steps back from f1 to e1.
beats.speak: Second, the king must never have moved. Here the king steps from E one to F one. Later it steps back from F one to E one.

beats.label: Gone for good
beats.say: It looks just as before, but this king has moved. It can never castle again, on either side, for the rest of the game.
beats.speak: It looks just as before, but this king has moved. It can never castle again, on either side, for the rest of the game.

beats.label: Rule three: the rook has not moved
beats.say: Third, the rook must never have moved either. The rook goes from h1 to h3. Later it comes back from h3 to h1.
beats.speak: Third, the rook must never have moved either. The rook goes from H one to H three. Later it comes back from H three to H one.

beats.label: The other rook still counts
beats.say: White can never castle with this h1 rook now. But the a1 rook and the king have stayed at home, so queenside castling is still possible.
beats.speak: White can never castle with this H one rook now. But the A one rook and the king have stayed at home, so queenside castling is still possible.

beats.label: Rule four: not out of check
beats.say: Fourth, you cannot castle while your king is in check. The bishop on b4 attacks the king on e1, so White must answer the check another way.
beats.speak: Fourth, you cannot castle while your king is in check. The bishop on B four attacks the king on E one, so White must answer the check another way.

beats.label: Rule five: not through check
beats.say: Fifth, the king may not cross an attacked square. The bishop on c4 attacks f1, the square the king passes over, so kingside castling is not allowed.
beats.speak: Fifth, the king may not cross an attacked square. The bishop on C four attacks F one, the square the king passes over, so kingside castling is not allowed.

beats.label: Rule six: not into check
beats.say: Sixth, the king may not land in check. The rook on g6 attacks g1 down the open g-file, so the king cannot castle onto it.
beats.speak: Sixth, the king may not land in check. The rook on G six attacks G one down the open g-file, so the king cannot castle onto it.

beats.label: Attacks can go away
beats.say: These check rules only matter at the moment you castle. The black rook moves from g6 to a6, and now nothing attacks e1, f1 or g1, so White may castle.
beats.speak: These check rules only matter at the moment you castle. The black rook moves from G six to A six, and now nothing attacks E one, F one or G one, so White may castle.

beats.label: The queenside exception
beats.say: On the queenside the king crosses d1 and lands on c1, so those squares must be safe. But b1 is different: only the rook passes over it, so it may be attacked.
beats.speak: On the queenside the king crosses D one and lands on C one, so those squares must be safe. But B one is different: only the rook passes over it, so it may be attacked.

beats.label: Castling anyway
beats.say: So White may castle here. First the king slides across from e1 to c1. Then the rook hops over it from a1 to d1, straight across the attacked b1 square.
beats.speak: So White may castle here. First the king slides across from E one to C one. Then the rook hops over it from A one to D one, straight across the attacked B one square.

beats.label: The same for Black
beats.say: The same holds for Black. The bishop on e5 attacks b8, but c8, d8 and e8 are safe, so Black may still castle on the queenside.
beats.speak: The same holds for Black. The bishop on E five attacks B eight, but C eight, D eight and E eight are safe, so Black may still castle on the queenside.

beats.label: A castling checklist
beats.say: Before castling, ask: is the path empty? Have the king and this rook stayed at home? Is the king safe now, on the way and where it lands? If every answer is yes, you may castle.
beats.speak: Before castling, ask: is the path empty? Have the king and this rook stayed at home? Is the king safe now, on the way and where it lands? If every answer is yes, you may castle.

beats.label: Your turn
beats.say: Now try it yourself. Work out which way White may castle in this position, then castle and play on.
beats.speak: Now try it yourself. Work out which way White may castle in this position, then castle and play on.

lessons.title: Promotion and En Passant
teaches: A pawn that reaches the far rank is promoted at once to a queen, rook, bishop or knight of its own colour.
Most players choose a queen, but sometimes a knight is better.
A pawn can promote by moving straight ahead or by capturing.
If an opposing pawn makes a double step and lands beside your pawn, you may take it en passant, as though it had moved just one square.
En passant is allowed only on the very next move.

practice.goal: Capture the pawn on d5 en passant, then race a pawn to the eighth rank and promote it.
hints: En passant comes with a time limit: you may capture a pawn that has just made a double step only on the very next move, never later.
Your pawn on e5 stands right beside the black pawn on d5. Look at the square the black pawn passed over.
practice.offTrack: That move lets the en passant chance go for good. Undo it and capture the pawn on d5 first, by moving your e5 pawn onto the square it passed over.

mistakes.a6a7: Your a-pawn can race later. En passant must be played at once or the chance is gone, so undo this and capture the d5 pawn in passing first.
mistakes.e5e6: Pushing past the black pawn throws the en passant chance away. Undo it and capture the pawn on d5 in passing first.

practice.success: Well done: you captured en passant and promoted a pawn, so you have used both special pawn rules. Play on with your new piece.

beats.label: Two special pawn rules
beats.say: Pawns have two special rules. Promotion rewards a pawn that marches all the way, and en passant is a surprising capture.
beats.speak: Pawns have two special rules. Promotion rewards a pawn that marches all the way, and en passant is a surprising capture.

beats.label: Nearly there
beats.say: This white pawn steps from b6 to b7. Now it is one square from the eighth rank, the far end of the board.
beats.speak: This white pawn steps from B six to B seven. Now it is one square from the eighth rank, the far end of the board.

beats.label: Becoming a queen
beats.say: The pawn steps to b8 and is changed at once into a queen. This is called promotion.
beats.speak: The pawn steps to B eight and is changed at once into a queen. This is called promotion.

beats.label: Four choices
beats.say: The player picks the new piece: a queen, rook, bishop or knight, always of the pawn's own colour. Turning into a king is never allowed, and neither is remaining a pawn.
beats.speak: The player picks the new piece: a queen, rook, bishop or knight, always of the pawn's own colour. Turning into a king is never allowed, and neither is remaining a pawn.

beats.label: Usually a queen
beats.say: Most players choose a queen, the strongest piece. You may promote even while your first queen is still on the board: this pawn becomes a queen on g8, so White now has two queens.
beats.speak: Most players choose a queen, the strongest piece. You may promote even while your first queen is still on the board: this pawn becomes a queen on G eight, so White now has two queens.

beats.label: Black promotes on rank 1
beats.say: Black's pawns promote when they reach the first rank. This black pawn steps from f2 to f1 and becomes a black queen.
beats.speak: Black's pawns promote when they reach the first rank. This black pawn steps from F two to F one and becomes a black queen.

beats.label: Promoting with a capture
beats.say: A pawn can also promote by capturing. The way ahead to c8 is blocked, so this pawn takes the rook on d8 and becomes a queen there.
beats.speak: A pawn can also promote by capturing. The way ahead to C eight is blocked, so this pawn takes the rook on D eight and becomes a queen there.

beats.label: When a knight is better
beats.say: Sometimes a knight is the better choice. This pawn on f7 is about to reach f8.
beats.speak: Sometimes a knight is the better choice. This pawn on F seven is about to reach F eight.

beats.label: A knight fork
beats.say: It becomes a knight on f8. The knight attacks the black king on e6 and the black queen on h7 at the same time. A queen on f8 would attack neither.
beats.speak: It becomes a knight on F eight. The knight attacks the black king on E six and the black queen on H seven at the same time. A queen on F eight would attack neither.

beats.label: Winning the queen
beats.say: The black king must move out of check, and here it steps from e6 to e5. Then White's knight takes the queen, moving from f8 to h7.
beats.speak: The black king must move out of check, and here it steps from E six to E five. Then White's knight takes the queen, moving from F eight to H seven.

beats.label: En passant
beats.say: Now the second rule. A white pawn stands on f5, and a black pawn waits on g7, still on its starting square.
beats.speak: Now the second rule. A white pawn stands on F five, and a black pawn waits on G seven, still on its starting square.

beats.label: A double step past
beats.say: Black's pawn makes a double step, from g7 to g5. It lands right beside the white pawn.
beats.speak: Black's pawn makes a double step, from G seven to G five. It lands right beside the white pawn.

beats.label: Slipping past
beats.say: Had it stepped only to g6, the white pawn could have captured it there. With its double step, it tried to slip past.
beats.speak: Had it stepped only to G six, the white pawn could have captured it there. With its double step, it tried to slip past.

beats.label: Capturing in passing
beats.say: White may capture it anyway, as if it had moved one square. White's pawn moves from f5 to g6, and the black pawn on g5 is taken off the board.
beats.speak: White may capture it anyway, as if it had moved one square. White's pawn moves from F five to G six, and the black pawn on G five is taken off the board.

beats.label: In passing
beats.say: The name en passant is French and means in passing. Only pawns can make this capture, and only pawns can be taken this way.
beats.speak: The name en passant is French and means in passing. Only pawns can make this capture, and only pawns can be taken this way.

beats.label: Only straight away
beats.say: En passant must be played at once. Black's pawn makes a double step, from g7 to g5. White's pawn moves from h2 to h3 instead.
beats.speak: En passant must be played at once. Black's pawn makes a double step, from G seven to G five. White's pawn moves from H two to H three instead.

beats.label: Too late
beats.say: Black's pawn moves from b7 to b6. The chance is gone for good: the pawn on f5 can no longer capture the pawn on g5.
beats.speak: Black's pawn moves from B seven to B six. The chance is gone for good: the pawn on F five can no longer capture the pawn on G five.

beats.label: Only after a double step
beats.say: This black pawn steps one square, from g6 to g5. It did not make a double step, so en passant is not allowed here.
beats.speak: This black pawn steps one square, from G six to G five. It did not make a double step, so en passant is not allowed here.

beats.label: Black can do it too
beats.say: Black can capture en passant too. White's pawn makes a double step, from b2 to b4. Black's pawn on c4 captures it in passing by moving to b3.
beats.speak: Black can capture en passant too. White's pawn makes a double step, from B two to B four. Black's pawn on C four captures it in passing by moving to B three.

beats.label: Try it yourself
beats.say: Now try both rules. Black's pawn has just made a double step to d5. Capture it en passant, then race a pawn to the eighth rank and promote it.
beats.speak: Now try both rules. Black's pawn has just made a double step to D five. Capture it en passant, then race a pawn to the eighth rank and promote it.

lessons.title: Draws
teaches: A draw means neither player wins; each usually scores half a point.
Stalemate: the player to move is not in check and has no legal move. The game is drawn at once.
When neither side can possibly give checkmate, such as king against king, the game is drawn.
The same position three times, or fifty moves each without a capture or pawn move, lets the player to move claim a draw.
Five times the same position, or seventy-five moves each without a capture or pawn move, ends the game as a draw automatically.
Players may also agree to a draw.

beats.label: Not every game is won
beats.say: Not every chess game has a winner. When a game is drawn, nobody wins, and in a tournament each player usually scores half a point.
beats.speak: Not every chess game has a winner. When a game is drawn, nobody wins, and in a tournament each player usually scores half a point.

beats.label: Five kinds of draw
beats.say: A game can be drawn in five main ways: stalemate, not enough pieces to checkmate, repeating a position, a long run of moves with no capture or pawn move, and agreement.
beats.speak: A game can be drawn in five main ways: stalemate, not enough pieces to checkmate, repeating a position, a long run of moves with no capture or pawn move, and agreement.

beats.label: A winning position
beats.say: Here Black has only a king left, while White has a king and a queen. White should win, but must be careful.
beats.speak: Here Black has only a king left, while White has a king and a queen. White should win, but must be careful.

beats.label: White moves the queen
beats.say: White's queen moves from c5 to c7. Now it is Black's turn.
beats.speak: White's queen moves from C five to C seven. Now it is Black's turn.

beats.label: No legal move
beats.say: Black's king on a8 is not in check. But the queen attacks a7, b7 and b8, so the king has nowhere to go, and Black has no other piece to move.
beats.speak: Black's king on A eight is not in check. But the queen attacks A seven, B seven and B eight, so the king has nowhere to go, and Black has no other piece to move.

beats.label: Stalemate
beats.say: This is stalemate. When the player to move is not in check but has no legal move, the game ends at once as a draw.
beats.speak: This is stalemate. When the player to move is not in check but has no legal move, the game ends at once as a draw.

beats.label: Check or no check
beats.say: How is this different from checkmate? A checkmated king is attacked and has no escape. Here the king is not attacked at all; Black simply has no move to play.
beats.speak: How is this different from checkmate? A checkmated king is attacked and has no escape. Here the king is not attacked at all; Black simply has no move to play.

beats.label: Blocked pawns count too
beats.say: Stalemate can happen with other pieces still on the board. If it is Black's turn here, the pawn on a5 is blocked by White's pawn on a4, and every square around the king is attacked.
beats.speak: Stalemate can happen with other pieces still on the board. If it is Black's turn here, the pawn on A five is blocked by White's pawn on A four, and every square around the king is attacked.

beats.label: Another stalemate
beats.say: Black's king on h8 is not in check, and Black has no legal move, so this is stalemate too. When you are winning, make sure each move leaves your opponent a legal move, unless your move is checkmate.
beats.speak: Black's king on H eight is not in check, and Black has no legal move, so this is stalemate too. When you are winning, make sure each move leaves your opponent a legal move, unless your move is checkmate.

beats.label: Not enough material
beats.say: A game is also drawn when neither side can possibly give checkmate. With only two kings left, checkmate can never happen, so the game is over.
beats.speak: A game is also drawn when neither side can possibly give checkmate. With only two kings left, checkmate can never happen, so the game is over.

beats.label: A lone bishop or knight
beats.say: A king and one bishop cannot checkmate a lone king, and neither can a king and one knight. These games are drawn as well.
beats.speak: A king and one bishop cannot checkmate a lone king, and neither can a king and one knight. These games are drawn as well.

beats.label: A pawn is different
beats.say: A single pawn is a different story. It might reach the last rank and become a queen, so the game goes on.
beats.speak: A single pawn is a different story. It might reach the last rank and become a queen, so the game goes on.

beats.label: Repeating a position
beats.say: Now a draw by repetition. Black has two rooks and a knight against White's queen, so Black is ahead. White's best hope is to keep giving check.
beats.speak: Now a draw by repetition. Black has two rooks and a knight against White's queen, so Black is ahead. White's best hope is to keep giving check.

beats.label: The position appears once
beats.say: White's queen moves from d7 to e8, giving check. Black's king steps from g8 to h7. Remember this position.
beats.speak: White's queen moves from D seven to E eight, giving check. Black's king steps from G eight to H seven. Remember this position.

beats.label: The position appears twice
beats.say: White's queen checks from e4. Black's king goes back to g8. White's queen checks from e8 again. Black's king returns to h7. The same position has appeared a second time.
beats.speak: White's queen checks from E four. Black's king goes back to G eight. White's queen checks from E eight again. Black's king returns to H seven. The same position has appeared a second time.

beats.label: The position appears three times
beats.say: White's queen checks from e4. Black's king goes to g8. White's queen checks from e8. Black's king goes to h7. This is the third time.
beats.speak: White's queen checks from E four. Black's king goes to G eight. White's queen checks from E eight. Black's king goes to H seven. This is the third time.

beats.label: Claiming the draw
beats.say: A position counts as repeated only if the same side is to move and the same moves are available, castling included. After three such repeats, the player to move can claim a draw, even if they were not in a row.
beats.speak: A position counts as repeated only if the same side is to move and the same moves are available, castling included. After three such repeats, the player to move can claim a draw, even if they were not in a row.

beats.label: Five times ends it
beats.say: If nobody claims, play goes on. But if the same position appears five times, the game is drawn automatically.
beats.speak: If nobody claims, play goes on. But if the same position appears five times, the game is drawn automatically.

beats.label: The fifty-move rule
beats.say: Another rule stops endless games. If each player makes fifty moves with no capture and no pawn move, the player whose turn it is may claim a draw.
beats.speak: Another rule stops endless games. If each player makes fifty moves with no capture and no pawn move, the player whose turn it is may claim a draw.

beats.label: Seventy-five moves
beats.say: After seventy-five moves each with no capture and no pawn move, the game is drawn automatically, unless the last move gave checkmate.
beats.speak: After seventy-five moves each with no capture and no pawn move, the game is drawn automatically, unless the last move gave checkmate.

beats.label: Agreeing a draw
beats.say: Finally, once both have made a move, the players can agree to a draw, though some events limit this. Offer it just after making your move; your opponent may accept, or decline by playing on.
beats.speak: Finally, once both have made a move, the players can agree to a draw, though some events limit this. Offer it just after making your move; your opponent may accept, or decline by playing on.

beats.label: Draws in summary
beats.say: So a game can end in a draw by stalemate, not enough material, repetition, the fifty-move rule or agreement. A draw is half a point: much better than a loss.
beats.speak: So a game can end in a draw by stalemate, not enough material, repetition, the fifty-move rule or agreement. A draw is half a point: much better than a loss.

lessons.title: Piece Values
teaches: A pawn is worth 1 point, a knight 3, a bishop 3, a rook 5 and a queen 9.
The king has no point value: if it is checkmated, the game is lost.
Each army starts with 39 points of material.
Values help you judge a trade: compare what you give with what you get.
Checkmate matters more than points.

beats.label: Pieces have different strengths
beats.say: Some pieces are stronger than others. To compare them quickly, chess players give each piece a value in points.
beats.speak: Some pieces are stronger than others. To compare them quickly, chess players give each piece a value in points.

beats.label: The pawn: 1
beats.say: A pawn is worth one point. It is the smallest unit, so the other values are counted in pawns.
beats.speak: A pawn is worth one point. It is the smallest unit, so the other values are counted in pawns.

beats.label: The knight: 3
beats.say: A knight is worth three points, about the same as three pawns.
beats.speak: A knight is worth three points, about the same as three pawns.

beats.label: The bishop: 3
beats.say: A bishop is also worth three points. Knights and bishops are called minor pieces, and they are roughly equal.
beats.speak: A bishop is also worth three points. Knights and bishops are called minor pieces, and they are roughly equal.

beats.label: The rook: 5
beats.say: A rook is worth five points, more than a knight or a bishop.
beats.speak: A rook is worth five points, more than a knight or a bishop.

beats.label: The queen: 9
beats.say: The queen is worth nine points. She combines the moves of a rook and a bishop, so she is the strongest piece.
beats.speak: The queen is worth nine points. She combines the moves of a rook and a bishop, so she is the strongest piece.

beats.label: The king has no price
beats.say: The king has no point value. It can never be traded or captured, and if your king is checkmated, you lose the game.
beats.speak: The king has no point value. It can never be traded or captured, and if your king is checkmated, you lose the game.

beats.label: A whole army
beats.say: At the start, each side has eight pawns, two knights, two bishops, two rooks and a queen. Add them up and each army is worth 39 points.
beats.speak: At the start, each side has eight pawns, two knights, two bishops, two rooks and a queen. Add them up and each army is worth 39 points.

beats.label: An even trade
beats.say: Values help you judge trades. Here White can capture the knight on c6, and Black can capture back.
beats.speak: Values help you judge trades. Here White can capture the knight on C six, and Black can capture back.

beats.label: Bishop for knight
beats.say: White's bishop captures the knight on c6. Black's pawn on b7 captures the bishop.
beats.speak: White's bishop captures the knight on C six. Black's pawn on B seven captures the bishop.

beats.label: Three for three
beats.say: Each side gave up three points. That is an even trade: nobody gained anything.
beats.speak: Each side gave up three points. That is an even trade: nobody gained anything.

beats.label: A bad trade
beats.say: Here White's rook can take the knight on d5, but Black's pawn on e6 guards it.
beats.speak: Here White's rook can take the knight on D five, but Black's pawn on E six guards it.

beats.label: Rook for knight
beats.say: White's rook captures the knight on d5. Black's pawn captures the rook. White gave five points and got only three back, losing two.
beats.speak: White's rook captures the knight on D five. Black's pawn captures the rook. White gave five points and got only three back, losing two.

beats.label: A good trade
beats.say: This time White's knight can take a rook on e5 that is guarded by the pawn on d6.
beats.speak: This time White's knight can take a rook on E five that is guarded by the pawn on D six.

beats.label: Knight for rook
beats.say: White's knight captures the rook on e5. Black's pawn captures the knight. White gave three points and won five, gaining two points in the trade.
beats.speak: White's knight captures the rook on E five. Black's pawn captures the knight. White gave three points and won five, gaining two points in the trade.

beats.label: Points are not everything
beats.say: Look at this position. Black has a whole extra queen, nine points more than White. But it is White's turn.
beats.speak: Look at this position. Black has a whole extra queen, nine points more than White. But it is White's turn.

beats.label: Mate beats material
beats.say: White's rook moves from e1 to e8. It is checkmate: the king cannot escape, and nothing can block or capture the rook.
beats.speak: White's rook moves from E one to E eight. It is checkmate: the king cannot escape, and nothing can block or capture the rook.

beats.label: Values guide you
beats.say: So use piece values to judge trades and captures, but always look for checks and checkmates first. Checkmate decides the game, not points.
beats.speak: So use piece values to judge trades and captures, but always look for checks and checkmates first. Checkmate decides the game, not points.

lessons.title: Counting Material
teaches: To count material, add up the points of each side's pieces, leaving out the kings.
A fair trade gives up as many points as it wins; an unfair trade gives up more.
Before capturing, count the attackers and the defenders of the target.
Capture with your least valuable piece first.
More attackers than defenders usually wins material, but check the values too.

beats.label: Who is ahead?
beats.say: During a game it helps to know who has more material: more pieces, by value. You find out by counting points.
beats.speak: During a game it helps to know who has more material: more pieces, by value. You find out by counting points.

beats.label: White's material
beats.say: Start with White. A queen is nine, a rook five, a knight three, and five pawns make five more. White has 22 points.
beats.speak: Start with White. A queen is nine, a rook five, a knight three, and five pawns make five more. White has 22 points.

beats.label: Black's material
beats.say: Now Black. Two rooks make ten, a bishop and a knight add six, and five pawns add five. Black has 21 points.
beats.speak: Now Black. Two rooks make ten, a bishop and a knight add six, and five pawns add five. Black has 21 points.

beats.label: The difference
beats.say: White has one point more: White is a pawn ahead. Kings are never counted, because each side always has one.
beats.speak: White has one point more: White is a pawn ahead. Kings are never counted, because each side always has one.

beats.label: A fair trade
beats.say: Counting also shows whether a trade is fair. Here Black is five points ahead, and White's rook can take the rook on d8.
beats.speak: Counting also shows whether a trade is fair. Here Black is five points ahead, and White's rook can take the rook on D eight.

beats.label: Rook for rook
beats.say: White's rook captures the rook on d8. Black's rook on f8 captures back on d8.
beats.speak: White's rook captures the rook on D eight. Black's rook on F eight captures back on D eight.

beats.label: Still five ahead
beats.say: Each side lost five points, so the trade was fair. Black was five points ahead before it and is still five points ahead.
beats.speak: Each side lost five points, so the trade was fair. Black was five points ahead before it and is still five points ahead.

beats.label: An unfair trade
beats.say: Here White's bishop can take the pawn on f7, but Black's king guards that pawn.
beats.speak: Here White's bishop can take the pawn on F seven, but Black's king guards that pawn.

beats.label: Bishop for pawn
beats.say: White's bishop captures the pawn on f7, giving check. Black's king captures the bishop.
beats.speak: White's bishop captures the pawn on F seven, giving check. Black's king captures the bishop.

beats.label: Three for one
beats.say: White gave up three points to win one, so the trade lost two points. White was three points ahead before it, and now only one.
beats.speak: White gave up three points to win one, so the trade lost two points. White was three points ahead before it, and now only one.

beats.label: Attackers and defenders
beats.say: Before you capture, count. White's knight attacks the pawn on e5, and Black's knight on c6 defends it: one attacker, one defender.
beats.speak: Before you capture, count. White's knight attacks the pawn on E five, and Black's knight on C six defends it: one attacker, one defender.

beats.label: Taking too soon
beats.say: White's knight captures the pawn on e5. Black's knight captures the knight. White gave three points for one.
beats.speak: White's knight captures the pawn on E five. Black's knight captures the knight. White gave three points for one.

beats.label: Two attackers
beats.say: Now White has a rook on e1 as well. Two white pieces attack the pawn on e5, and only one black piece defends it.
beats.speak: Now White has a rook on E one as well. Two white pieces attack the pawn on E five, and only one black piece defends it.

beats.label: Cheapest piece first
beats.say: White's knight captures the pawn on e5. Black's knight captures the knight. White's rook captures the black knight on e5.
beats.speak: White's knight captures the pawn on E five. Black's knight captures the knight. White's rook captures the black knight on E five.

beats.label: Counting the result
beats.say: White gave a knight, three points, and won a pawn and a knight, four points: a gain of one point. Capturing first with the cheaper knight made that work.
beats.speak: White gave a knight, three points, and won a pawn and a knight, four points: a gain of one point. Capturing first with the cheaper knight made that work.

beats.label: Check the values too
beats.say: Numbers are not everything. Here one queen attacks the pawn on d5 and one pawn defends it. Taking would swap White's queen, worth nine, for a single pawn.
beats.speak: Numbers are not everything. Here one queen attacks the pawn on D five and one pawn defends it. Taking would swap White's queen, worth nine, for a single pawn.

beats.label: Count before you capture
beats.say: So count both armies to see who is ahead, compare what each trade gives and gets, and count attackers and defenders before every capture.
beats.speak: So count both armies to see who is ahead, compare what each trade gives and gets, and count attackers and defenders before every capture.

lessons.title: Chess Notation
teaches: Moves are written with square names: the file letter, then the rank number.
Each piece except the pawn has a capital letter: K, Q, R, B, and N for the knight.
x marks a capture, + marks check and # marks checkmate.
O-O is castling on the king's side and O-O-O castling on the queen's side.
A promotion adds the new piece, as in b8=Q; ! marks a good move and ? a mistake.

beats.label: Writing chess down
beats.say: Chess players can write down every move with a short code called notation. With it, any game can be recorded, shared and played through again.
beats.speak: Chess players can write down every move with a short code called notation. With it, any game can be recorded, shared and played through again.

beats.label: Square names
beats.say: Notation is built on square names: the file letter, then the rank number, just as in The Chessboard lesson. These two squares are d4 and f3.
beats.speak: Notation is built on square names: the file letter, then the rank number, just as in The Chessboard lesson. These two squares are D four and F three.

beats.label: Piece letters
beats.say: Every piece apart from the pawn is written with a capital letter. The king is K, the queen is Q, the rook is R and the bishop is B.
beats.speak: Every piece apart from the pawn is written with a capital letter. The king is K, the queen is Q, the rook is R and the bishop is B.

beats.label: N for knight
beats.say: The knight is written N, because K already stands for the king.
beats.speak: The knight is written N, because K already stands for the king.

beats.label: Pawns have no letter
beats.say: Pawns get no letter at all. A pawn move is just the square it lands on, so White's pawn going from d2 to d4 is written d4.
beats.speak: Pawns get no letter at all. A pawn move is just the square it lands on, so White's pawn going from D two to D four is written D four.

beats.label: A piece move
beats.say: Black answers with the knight from g8 to f6. A piece move is the piece's letter and then its new square: Nf6.
beats.speak: Black answers with the knight from G eight to F six. A piece move is the piece's letter and then its new square: N F six, meaning knight to F six.

beats.label: White's knight
beats.say: White brings a knight out, from b1 to c3. That is Nc3.
beats.speak: White brings a knight out, from B one to C three. That is N C three.

beats.label: Black's pawn
beats.say: Black's pawn steps from d7 to d5, written d5.
beats.speak: Black's pawn steps from D seven to D five, written D five.

beats.label: Move numbers
beats.say: A White move and Black's reply share one number. So far this game reads 1. d4 Nf6 2. Nc3 d5.
beats.speak: A White move and Black's reply share one number. So far this game reads: one, D four, knight F six. Two, knight C three, D five.

beats.label: The bishop comes out
beats.say: On move 3, White's bishop travels from c1 to g5. That is Bg5.
beats.speak: On move three, White's bishop travels from C one to G five. That is bishop G five.

beats.label: A quiet pawn move
beats.say: Black pushes a pawn from c7 to c6, written simply c6.
beats.speak: Black pushes a pawn from C seven to C six, written simply C six.

beats.label: Captures use x
beats.say: On move 4, White's bishop takes the knight on f6. A capture puts an x before the square: Bxf6, read as bishop takes f6.
beats.speak: On move four, White's bishop takes the knight on F six. A capture puts an x before the square: B x F six, read as bishop takes F six.

beats.label: Pawn captures
beats.say: Black's pawn on e7 takes the bishop back on f6. A pawn capture begins with the file the pawn left: exf6, read as e takes f6.
beats.speak: Black's pawn on E seven takes the bishop back on F six. A pawn capture begins with the file the pawn left: E x F six, read as E takes F six.

beats.label: Castling kingside
beats.say: Castling has its own sign. Here the king goes from e1 to g1. Then the rook hops over it from h1 to f1. Castling on the king's side is written O-O, and said as castles kingside.
beats.speak: Castling has its own sign. Here the king goes from E one to G one. Then the rook hops over it from H one to F one. Castling on the king's side is written O O, and said as castles kingside.

beats.label: Castling queenside
beats.say: On the queen's side, the king goes from e1 to c1. Then the rook hops from a1 to d1. That longer castling is written O-O-O, and said as castles queenside.
beats.speak: On the queen's side, the king goes from E one to C one. Then the rook hops from A one to D one. That longer castling is written O O O, and said as castles queenside.

beats.label: Check is +
beats.say: Here White's rook goes from a1 to a8 and checks the black king. A checking move ends with a plus sign: Ra8+.
beats.speak: Here White's rook goes from A one to A eight and checks the black king. A checking move ends with a plus sign: rook A eight, check.

beats.label: Checkmate is #
beats.say: Now White's rook goes from d2 to d8, and the black king has no escape. Checkmate is marked with a hash sign: Rd8#.
beats.speak: Now White's rook goes from D two to D eight, and the black king has no escape. Checkmate is marked with a hash sign: rook D eight, checkmate.

beats.label: Promotion
beats.say: This white pawn steps from b7 to b8 and becomes a queen. A promotion adds an equals sign and the new piece's letter: b8=Q.
beats.speak: This white pawn steps from B seven to B eight and becomes a queen. A promotion adds an equals sign and the new piece's letter: B eight equals Q, meaning it promotes to a queen.

beats.label: Good moves and mistakes
beats.say: Writers also add comments: ! after a good move and ? after a mistake. Two of them, !! or ??, mark a brilliant move or a serious blunder.
beats.speak: Writers also add comments: an exclamation mark after a good move, and a question mark after a mistake. Two exclamation marks mark a brilliant move, and two question marks a serious blunder.

beats.label: Which knight moved?
beats.say: Both White knights here could jump to d2, so Nd2 would not say which one went. The knight from b1 moves, so we add its file letter: Nbd2.
beats.speak: Both White knights here could jump to D two, so knight D two would not say which one went. The knight from B one moves, so we add its file letter: knight B, D two.

beats.label: Using the rank instead
beats.say: When the two pieces share a file, add the rank number instead. Both rooks could reach a3; the one from a1 moves, so it is written R1a3.
beats.speak: When the two pieces share a file, add the rank number instead. Both rooks could reach A three; the one from A one moves, so it is written rook one, A three.

beats.label: Read and write games
beats.say: Now you can read and write the moves of a whole game. Try writing down your next game move by move, then play it through again from the start.
beats.speak: Now you can read and write the moves of a whole game. Try writing down your next game move by move, then play it through again from the start.

lessons.title: Good Manners at the Board
teaches: Greet your opponent before the game and shake hands after it.
Stay quiet during play and let your opponent think in peace.
Touch-move: a piece of yours you touch on purpose must be moved; a piece of theirs you touch on purpose must be captured, if that is legal.
To straighten a piece, say "I'm adjusting" first, and only on your turn.
Resign politely, win modestly, lose graciously, and tidy the pieces away.

beats.label: Two people, one game
beats.say: Chess is played between two people. Good manners make the game pleasant for both of you, whoever wins.
beats.speak: Chess is played between two people. Good manners make the game pleasant for both of you, whoever wins.

beats.label: Greet your opponent
beats.say: Before the first move, greet your opponent, shake hands if that is the custom, and wish them a good game.
beats.speak: Before the first move, greet your opponent, shake hands if that is the custom, and wish them a good game.

beats.label: Quiet, please
beats.say: During the game, stay quiet. Don't chat, hum, tap the table or comment on your opponent's moves.
beats.speak: During the game, stay quiet. Don't chat, hum, tap the table or comment on your opponent's moves.

beats.label: Time to think
beats.say: Your opponent is thinking as hard as you are. Let them take their time, and keep your eyes on the board.
beats.speak: Your opponent is thinking as hard as you are. Let them take their time, and keep your eyes on the board.

beats.label: Touch-move: your pieces
beats.say: Serious games use the touch-move rule. Touch one of your own pieces on purpose, and you must move it, as long as it has a legal move.
beats.speak: Serious games use the touch-move rule. Touch one of your own pieces on purpose, and you must move it, as long as it has a legal move.

beats.label: Think with your hands still
beats.say: So decide on your move before you reach for a piece. Here, touching the knight on g1 means the knight must move.
beats.speak: So decide on your move before you reach for a piece. Here, touching the knight on G one means the knight must move.

beats.label: A few moves in
beats.say: White pushes a pawn from c2 to c4. Black answers with a pawn from d7 to d5.
beats.speak: White pushes a pawn from C two to C four. Black answers with a pawn from D seven to D five.

beats.label: Touching your opponent's piece
beats.say: The rule covers your opponent's pieces too. If White touches the pawn on d5 on purpose, White must capture it, because capturing it is legal.
beats.speak: The rule covers your opponent's pieces too. If White touches the pawn on D five on purpose, White must capture it, because capturing it is legal.

beats.label: Letting go
beats.say: Once you let go of a piece on a legal square, the move is made and cannot be taken back. Castling is complete once the rook is placed too, and a promotion once the new piece stands on the pawn's square.
beats.speak: Once you let go of a piece on a legal square, the move is made and cannot be taken back. Castling is complete once the rook is placed too, and a promotion once the new piece stands on the pawn's square.

beats.label: Straightening a piece
beats.say: Sometimes a piece sits crooked on its square. On your turn, first say "I'm adjusting", or the French "j'adoube", then straighten it. That warns your opponent you are not choosing that piece to move.
beats.speak: Sometimes a piece sits crooked on its square. On your turn, first say "I'm adjusting", or the French "zhah-doob", then straighten it. That warns your opponent you are not choosing that piece to move.

beats.label: Accidents
beats.say: Touch-move is about touching a piece on purpose. If your sleeve knocks a piece by accident, put it back, and the rule does not apply.
beats.speak: Touch-move is about touching a piece on purpose. If your sleeve knocks a piece by accident, put it back, and the rule does not apply.

beats.label: Resigning
beats.say: If your position is hopeless, you may resign instead of playing on. Say clearly "I resign" and offer your hand.
beats.speak: If your position is hopeless, you may resign instead of playing on. Say clearly "I resign" and offer your hand.

beats.label: No need to give up
beats.say: You never have to resign. Playing on is fine while you still have chances, and games between beginners often turn around.
beats.speak: You never have to resign. Playing on is fine while you still have chances, and games between beginners often turn around.

beats.label: Winning kindly
beats.say: When you win, shake hands and say "good game". Don't cheer loudly or tease your opponent.
beats.speak: When you win, shake hands and say "good game". Don't cheer loudly or tease your opponent.

beats.label: Losing well
beats.say: When you lose, shake hands too and congratulate your opponent. Every loss teaches you something for next time.
beats.speak: When you lose, shake hands too and congratulate your opponent. Every loss teaches you something for next time.

beats.label: Talking it over
beats.say: Afterwards you might look through the game together. Do it quietly, away from anyone still playing.
beats.speak: Afterwards you might look through the game together. Do it quietly, away from anyone still playing.

beats.label: Tidy up
beats.say: Finally, set the pieces back up on their starting squares, ready for whoever plays next.
beats.speak: Finally, set the pieces back up on their starting squares, ready for whoever plays next.

beats.label: Good manners in short
beats.say: Greet, stay quiet, follow touch-move, say "I'm adjusting" before straightening a piece, and be kind whether you win or lose.
beats.speak: Greet, stay quiet, follow touch-move, say "I'm adjusting" before straightening a piece, and be kind whether you win or lose.

lessons.title: Playing in a Tournament
teaches: A tournament is played in rounds, and the pairings say whom you play and with which colour.
A win scores 1 point, a draw half a point, a loss nothing.
Move, then press your clock with the same hand you moved with.
In most longer games you write down every move after you make it.
If there is a problem, pause the clock and call the arbiter rather than arguing.

beats.label: A chess competition
beats.say: A tournament is a competition with many players. Everyone plays several games, one in each round.
beats.speak: A tournament is a competition with many players. Everyone plays several games, one in each round.

beats.label: Rounds and pairings
beats.say: Before each round, the organisers publish the pairings: who plays whom, on which board, and who has the white pieces.
beats.speak: Before each round, the organisers publish the pairings: who plays whom, on which board, and who has the white pieces.

beats.label: Scoring
beats.say: A win scores one point, a draw half a point, and a loss nothing. The player with the most points at the end wins the tournament.
beats.speak: A win scores one point, a draw half a point, and a loss nothing. The player with the most points at the end wins the tournament.

beats.label: Meeting similar scores
beats.say: Many tournaments use the Swiss system. Players are not knocked out; in each round they meet opponents with similar scores.
beats.speak: Many tournaments use the Swiss system. Players are not knocked out; in each round they meet opponents with similar scores.

beats.label: Be on time
beats.say: Find your board and sit down before the round begins. If you arrive too late, you can lose the game without playing a move.
beats.speak: Find your board and sit down before the round begins. If you arrive too late, you can lose the game without playing a move.

beats.label: The chess clock
beats.say: Tournament games use a chess clock: two clocks joined together, one counting down your time and one counting down your opponent's.
beats.speak: Tournament games use a chess clock: two clocks joined together, one counting down your time and one counting down your opponent's.

beats.label: White's clock runs first
beats.say: When the game begins, White's clock is running. White opens by pushing a pawn from d2 to d4. White's clock keeps running until White presses it.
beats.speak: When the game begins, White's clock is running. White opens by pushing a pawn from D two to D four. White's clock keeps running until White presses it.

beats.label: Press after moving
beats.say: After moving, White presses the clock, which stops White's time and starts Black's. Black replies by pushing a pawn from d7 to d5, then presses the clock in turn.
beats.speak: After moving, White presses the clock, which stops White's time and starts Black's. Black replies by pushing a pawn from D seven to D five, then presses the clock in turn.

beats.label: Same hand
beats.say: Move the piece and press the clock with the same hand. Keep your other hand away from the clock.
beats.speak: Move the piece and press the clock with the same hand. Keep your other hand away from the clock.

beats.label: Running out of time
beats.say: If your time runs out, you lose, unless your opponent could not possibly checkmate you. Then the game is a draw.
beats.speak: If your time runs out, you lose, unless your opponent could not possibly checkmate you. Then the game is a draw.

beats.label: Writing the moves
beats.say: In most longer games, each player writes down every move of both sides on a scoresheet, using chess notation. In rapid games, or when very short of time, you may not have to.
beats.speak: In most longer games, each player writes down every move of both sides on a scoresheet, using chess notation. In rapid games, or when very short of time, you may not have to.

beats.label: Move, then write
beats.say: Make your move on the board first, then write it down. Here the scoresheet would show move one as d4 for White and d5 for Black.
beats.speak: Make your move on the board first, then write it down. Here the scoresheet would show move one as D four for White and D five for Black.

beats.label: The arbiter
beats.say: Every tournament has an arbiter, the referee. The arbiter makes sure the rules are followed and settles any problem.
beats.speak: Every tournament has an arbiter, the referee. The arbiter makes sure the rules are followed and settles any problem.

beats.label: Calling the arbiter
beats.say: If something goes wrong, such as an illegal move, a faulty clock or a draw claim, pause the clock and call the arbiter. Never argue with your opponent.
beats.speak: If something goes wrong, such as an illegal move, a faulty clock or a draw claim, pause the clock and call the arbiter. Never argue with your opponent.

beats.label: No outside help
beats.say: During play, you may not get advice from anyone, use notes or books, or analyse on another board. Check the rules on phones: they are normally not allowed with you at all, unless the event allows them, for example switched off in a bag.
beats.speak: During play, you may not get advice from anyone, use notes or books, or analyse on another board. Check the rules on phones: they are normally not allowed with you at all, unless the event allows them, for example switched off in a bag.

beats.label: Behaving well
beats.say: Walk quietly, and never talk about a game while it is being played. When you finish, leave the playing area so others can concentrate.
beats.speak: Walk quietly, and never talk about a game while it is being played. When you finish, leave the playing area so others can concentrate.

beats.label: After the game
beats.say: When the game ends, shake hands, both sign the scoresheets, and report the result as the organisers ask.
beats.speak: When the game ends, shake hands, both sign the scoresheets, and report the result as the organisers ask.

beats.label: Tournament checklist
beats.say: Check the pairings, arrive on time, press the clock with the hand you moved with, write the moves when the rules ask, and call the arbiter when you need help.
beats.speak: Check the pairings, arrive on time, press the clock with the hand you moved with, write the moves when the rules ask, and call the arbiter when you need help.

lessons.title: Rules Review
teaches: Each piece has its own way of moving; in ordinary moves, only the knight jumps over pieces.
Check must be answered at once: move the king, block, or capture the checker. Checkmate ends the game.
Castling, promotion and en passant are special moves with their own conditions.
Stalemate, not enough material, repetition, the fifty-move rule and agreement are draws.
Before every move, ask what your opponent's last move threatens and whether your piece will be safe.

beats.label: A quick tour
beats.say: This lesson gathers every rule you have learned into one quick tour, ending with two habits to use before each move.
beats.speak: This lesson gathers every rule you have learned into one quick tour, ending with two habits to use before each move.

beats.label: The pawn
beats.say: A pawn moves straight forward one square, or two from its starting square. It captures one square diagonally forward, so this pawn could take the knight on d3.
beats.speak: A pawn moves straight forward one square, or two from its starting square. It captures one square diagonally forward, so this pawn could take the knight on D three.

beats.label: The rook
beats.say: A rook moves any distance along its rank or file, as long as the path is clear.
beats.speak: A rook moves any distance along its rank or file, as long as the path is clear.

beats.label: The bishop
beats.say: A bishop moves any distance along a diagonal, so it always stays on squares of one colour.
beats.speak: A bishop moves any distance along a diagonal, so it always stays on squares of one colour.

beats.label: The queen
beats.say: The queen combines rook and bishop moves: she travels any distance along a rank, a file or a diagonal.
beats.speak: The queen combines rook and bishop moves: she travels any distance along a rank, a file or a diagonal.

beats.label: The knight
beats.say: The knight jumps in an L shape: two squares one way, then one square to the side. In ordinary moves, it is the only piece that jumps over others.
beats.speak: The knight jumps in an L shape: two squares one way, then one square to the side. In ordinary moves, it is the only piece that jumps over others.

beats.label: The king
beats.say: The king steps one square in any direction, but never onto a square that is attacked.
beats.speak: The king steps one square in any direction, but never onto a square that is attacked.

beats.label: Check
beats.say: Black's king is in check from the rook on e1. A check is answered by moving the king, blocking, or capturing the checker. Here Black has only a king, so the king must move.
beats.speak: Black's king is in check from the rook on E one. A check is answered by moving the king, blocking, or capturing the checker. Here Black has only a king, so the king must move.

beats.label: Checkmate
beats.say: White's queen moves from a7 to e7, giving check. The queen covers every square around the king, and the white king guards her. That is checkmate, and White wins.
beats.speak: White's queen moves from A seven to E seven, giving check. The queen covers every square around the king, and the white king guards her. That is checkmate, and White wins.

beats.label: Stalemate
beats.say: Suppose Black is to move here. The king is not attacked, yet it has nowhere to go and Black has nothing else to move: stalemate, a draw.
beats.speak: Suppose Black is to move here. The king is not attacked, yet it has nowhere to go and Black has nothing else to move: stalemate, a draw.

beats.label: Castling
beats.say: White castles kingside. The king moves two squares, from e1 to g1. Then the rook goes from h1 to f1, on the king's other side.
beats.speak: White castles kingside. The king moves two squares, from E one to G one. Then the rook goes from H one to F one, on the king's other side.

beats.label: When castling is allowed
beats.say: Castling needs all of this: neither the king nor that rook has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check, does not pass over an attacked square and does not finish on one.
beats.speak: Castling needs all of this: neither the king nor that rook has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check, does not pass over an attacked square and does not finish on one.

beats.label: Promotion
beats.say: White's pawn moves from b7 to b8 and becomes a queen. A pawn that reaches the last rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight.
beats.speak: White's pawn moves from B seven to B eight and becomes a queen. A pawn that reaches the last rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight.

beats.label: A two-square advance
beats.say: Black's pawn moves two squares, from d7 to d5, and lands right beside White's pawn on e5.
beats.speak: Black's pawn moves two squares, from D seven to D five, and lands right beside White's pawn on E five.

beats.label: Capturing in passing
beats.say: White's pawn captures en passant, moving from e5 to d6, and the black pawn on d5 is removed. This is allowed only on the very next move.
beats.speak: White's pawn captures en passant, moving from E five to D six, and the black pawn on D five is removed. This is allowed only on the very next move.

beats.label: Draws
beats.say: Remember the draws: stalemate, too little material to checkmate, a position repeated three times, fifty moves each with no capture or pawn move, and agreement. Repetition and fifty moves need a claim.
beats.speak: Remember the draws: stalemate, too little material to checkmate, a position repeated three times, fifty moves each with no capture or pawn move, and agreement. Repetition and fifty moves need a claim.

beats.label: What did they just do?
beats.say: Now two habits for every move. First, ask what your opponent's last move does. Does it attack one of your pieces, or threaten check?
beats.speak: Now two habits for every move. First, ask what your opponent's last move does. Does it attack one of your pieces, or threaten check?

beats.label: Is my piece safe?
beats.say: Second, check your own move before you play it. White's knight could jump to g5, but Black's pawn on h6 attacks that square.
beats.speak: Second, check your own move before you play it. White's knight could jump to G five, but Black's pawn on H six attacks that square.

beats.label: Look before you move
beats.say: Ask both questions before every move: what is my opponent threatening, and will my piece be safe? These two habits save more games than anything else.
beats.speak: Ask both questions before every move: what is my opponent threatening, and will my piece be safe? These two habits save more games than anything else.

lessons.title: Opening Principles
teaches: The opening is the first part of the game, when both sides get their pieces ready.
Pawns and pieces in the centre (d4, e4, d5, e5) control the most squares.
Develop your knights and bishops early.
Castle early to keep your king safe.
Move each piece once in the opening unless there is a good reason.
Clear the back rank so that your rooks are connected.

beats.label: What the opening is
beats.say: The opening is the first part of a game. Both sides bring their armies out, and a few simple ideas help you start well.
beats.speak: The opening is the first part of a game. Both sides bring their armies out, and a few simple ideas help you start well.

beats.label: The centre
beats.say: The four middle squares, d4, e4, d5 and e5, are the centre. Pawns and pieces that stand on them or aim at them have the most influence.
beats.speak: The four middle squares, D four, E four, D five and E five, are the centre. Pawns and pieces that stand on them or aim at them have the most influence.

beats.label: Pieces like the centre
beats.say: A knight in the centre on d4 reaches eight squares. The same knight in the corner on h1 reaches only two.
beats.speak: A knight in the centre on D four reaches eight squares. The same knight in the corner on H one reaches only two.

beats.label: A pawn takes the centre
beats.say: White begins by pushing the queen's pawn two squares, to d4. It claims a centre square and lets the bishop on c1 out.
beats.speak: White begins by pushing the queen's pawn two squares, to D four. It claims a centre square and lets the bishop on C one out.

beats.label: Black answers
beats.say: Black replies in the same way, with a pawn to d5. Each side now has a pawn in the centre.
beats.speak: Black replies in the same way, with a pawn to D five. Each side now has a pawn in the centre.

beats.label: Develop a knight
beats.say: Developing means bringing a piece to a square where it does useful work. White's knight jumps to f3, where it guards d4 and watches e5.
beats.speak: Developing means bringing a piece to a square where it does useful work. White's knight jumps to F three, where it guards D four and watches E five.

beats.label: Black's knight
beats.say: Black's knight jumps to f6. It guards d5 and watches e4.
beats.speak: Black's knight jumps to F six. It guards D five and watches E four.

beats.label: Develop a bishop
beats.say: White's dark-squared bishop goes out to f4. Black's light-squared bishop goes out to f5.
beats.speak: White's dark-squared bishop goes out to F four. Black's light-squared bishop goes out to F five.

beats.label: Opening a path
beats.say: White's e-pawn steps forward one square, to e3. Black's e-pawn steps to e6. Both moves open a diagonal for the other bishop.
beats.speak: White's e-pawn steps forward one square, to E three. Black's e-pawn steps to E six. Both moves open a diagonal for the other bishop.

beats.label: The last bishops
beats.say: White's bishop comes to e2. Black's bishop comes to e7. Now the squares between each king and its h-rook are empty.
beats.speak: White's bishop comes to E two. Black's bishop comes to E seven. Now the squares between each king and its h-rook are empty.

beats.label: Castle early
beats.say: White castles. The king goes two squares to g1. The rook hops over to f1.
beats.speak: White castles. The king goes two squares to G one. The rook hops over to F one.

beats.label: Why castling helps
beats.say: White's king now sits behind the pawns on f2, g2 and h2, away from the busy centre. The rook on f1 is ready to join the game.
beats.speak: White's king now sits behind the pawns on F two, G two and H two, away from the busy centre. The rook on F one is ready to join the game.

beats.label: Black castles too
beats.say: Black castles as well. The king goes to g8. The rook hops over to f8.
beats.speak: Black castles as well. The king goes to G eight. The rook hops over to F eight.

beats.label: A wandering knight
beats.say: Now a new game, to show what not to do. White's knight jumps to c3. Black's pawn advances to d5.
beats.speak: Now a new game, to show what not to do. White's knight jumps to C three. Black's pawn advances to D five.

beats.label: Chased away
beats.say: White's knight jumps again, to b5. Black's c-pawn steps to c6 and attacks it.
beats.speak: White's knight jumps again, to B five. Black's c-pawn steps to C six and attacks it.

beats.label: Back to the edge
beats.say: White's knight retreats to a3. Black's e-pawn advances to e5.
beats.speak: White's knight retreats to A three. Black's e-pawn advances to E five.

beats.label: Time lost
beats.say: White has spent three moves on one knight, which now sits on the edge. Black used the same three moves to put pawns on d5 and e5.
beats.speak: White has spent three moves on one knight, which now sits on the edge. Black used the same three moves to put pawns on D five and E five.

beats.label: Back to the first game
beats.say: Back to the first game, where both kings have castled. Every move there helped to claim the centre, bring out a piece or keep the king safe.
beats.speak: Back to the first game, where both kings have castled. Every move there helped to claim the centre, bring out a piece or keep the king safe.

beats.label: The other knights
beats.say: White's second knight comes to d2. Black's second knight comes to d7.
beats.speak: White's second knight comes to D two. Black's second knight comes to D seven.

beats.label: Room for the queens
beats.say: White's c-pawn steps to c3. Black's c-pawn steps to c6.
beats.speak: White's c-pawn steps to C three. Black's c-pawn steps to C six.

beats.label: Queens step up
beats.say: White's queen moves to c2. Black's queen moves to c7.
beats.speak: White's queen moves to C two. Black's queen moves to C seven.

beats.label: Connected rooks
beats.say: Now nothing stands between each side's two rooks. Rooks that see each other along the back rank are connected, and they guard each other.
beats.speak: Now nothing stands between each side's two rooks. Rooks that see each other along the back rank are connected, and they guard each other.

beats.label: The five ideas
beats.say: Take the centre, develop your knights and bishops, castle early, move each piece once unless there's a good reason, and connect your rooks. Then the middle of the game can begin.
beats.speak: Take the centre, develop your knights and bishops, castle early, move each piece once unless there's a good reason, and connect your rooks. Then the middle of the game can begin.

lessons.title: Scholar's Mate
teaches: Scholar's Mate is an early attack by a queen and a bishop on f7 (or on f2 against White).
At the start, f7 and f2 are guarded only by the king.
Defend f7 by blocking the attackers' lines or guarding it with another piece.
Develop with tempo: bring out pieces that attack the early queen.
An early queen attack is easy to stop if you stay calm and keep developing.

beats.label: A fast trap
beats.say: Scholar's Mate is a quick attack in which a queen and a bishop strike together at one weak square. Many beginners fall for it, so learn it and learn to stop it.
beats.speak: Scholar's Mate is a quick attack in which a queen and a bishop strike together at one weak square. Many beginners fall for it, so learn it and learn to stop it.

beats.label: The weak squares
beats.say: At the start, Black's pawn on f7 is guarded only by Black's king. White's pawn on f2 is guarded only by White's king.
beats.speak: At the start, Black's pawn on F seven is guarded only by Black's king. White's pawn on F two is guarded only by White's king.

beats.label: A quiet start
beats.say: White's e-pawn advances to e4. Black pushes the g-pawn one square, to g6, to make room for a bishop.
beats.speak: White's e-pawn advances to E four. Black pushes the g-pawn one square, to G six, to make room for a bishop.

beats.label: Both bishops come out
beats.say: White's bishop goes to c4 and aims at f7. Black's bishop goes to g7.
beats.speak: White's bishop goes to C four and aims at F seven. Black's bishop goes to G seven.

beats.label: The queen joins in
beats.say: White's queen comes out early, to f3. Now the queen and the bishop both aim at f7, and White threatens to take it with checkmate.
beats.speak: White's queen comes out early, to F three. Now the queen and the bishop both aim at F seven, and White threatens to take it with checkmate.

beats.label: A careless reply
beats.say: Black's knight jumps to c6. It is a useful developing move, but it does nothing about the threat to f7.
beats.speak: Black's knight jumps to C six. It is a useful developing move, but it does nothing about the threat to F seven.

beats.label: Checkmate on f7
beats.say: White's queen captures the pawn on f7. It is checkmate.
beats.speak: White's queen captures the pawn on F seven. It is checkmate.

beats.label: Why it is mate
beats.say: The king cannot take the queen, because the bishop on c4 guards her. No other black piece can reach her, and the only empty square beside the king, f8, is attacked. The game ended in four moves.
beats.speak: The king cannot take the queen, because the bishop on C four guards her. No other black piece can reach her, and the only empty square beside the king, F eight, is attacked. The game ended in four moves.

beats.label: Black can do it too
beats.say: The same idea works against White's pawn on f2. Suppose White starts slowly, with a pawn to a3. Black's e-pawn advances to e5.
beats.speak: The same idea works against White's pawn on F two. Suppose White starts slowly, with a pawn to A three. Black's e-pawn advances to E five.

beats.label: Black's bishop aims
beats.say: White pushes a pawn to h3. Black's bishop goes to c5 and aims at f2.
beats.speak: White pushes a pawn to H three. Black's bishop goes to C five and aims at F two.

beats.label: Black's queen aims
beats.say: White pushes a pawn to b3. Black's queen goes to f6 and aims at f2 as well.
beats.speak: White pushes a pawn to B three. Black's queen goes to F six and aims at F two as well.

beats.label: Checkmate on f2
beats.say: White pushes a pawn to g4 and ignores the danger. Black's queen captures on f2. It is checkmate.
beats.speak: White pushes a pawn to G four and ignores the danger. Black's queen captures on F two. It is checkmate.

beats.label: How to defend
beats.say: Back to White's attack, just after the queen came to f3. Black's pawn on f7 is attacked twice and guarded only once. Black must act now.
beats.speak: Back to White's attack, just after the queen came to F three. Black's pawn on F seven is attacked twice and guarded only once. Black must act now.

beats.label: Block the line
beats.say: A good answer: Black's knight jumps to f6. It develops a piece and stands in the queen's way, so she no longer attacks f7.
beats.speak: A good answer: Black's knight jumps to F six. It develops a piece and stands in the queen's way, so she no longer attacks F seven.

beats.label: Both sides develop
beats.say: White pushes the d-pawn to d3 to guard e4 from the knight. Black's other knight jumps to c6.
beats.speak: White pushes the d-pawn to D three to guard E four from the knight. Black's other knight jumps to C six.

beats.label: Develop with tempo
beats.say: White's knight goes to e2. Black's knight jumps to e5 and attacks both the queen and the bishop. A useful move that also makes a threat, so the opponent must react, is said to gain tempo.
beats.speak: White's knight goes to E two. Black's knight jumps to E five and attacks both the queen and the bishop. A useful move that also makes a threat, so the opponent must react, is said to gain tempo.

beats.label: Who is better now
beats.say: White's queen has to move again, while Black's pieces keep arriving with threats. The early queen has cost White time, and f7 is well guarded.
beats.speak: White's queen has to move again, while Black's pieces keep arriving with threats. The early queen has cost White time, and F seven is well guarded.

beats.label: Another simple defence
beats.say: Back once more to the moment the queen came to f3. This time Black's e-pawn steps to e6 and cuts the bishop's line to f7.
beats.speak: Back once more to the moment the queen came to F three. This time Black's e-pawn steps to E six and cuts the bishop's line to F seven.

beats.label: Only one attacker
beats.say: Now only the queen attacks f7, and the king guards it. If the queen captured there, the king would simply capture her.
beats.speak: Now only the queen attacks F seven, and the king guards it. If the queen captured there, the king would simply capture her.

beats.label: Don't panic
beats.say: An early queen attack looks frightening, but it is easy to meet. Guard f7, keep developing, and chase the queen with your pieces when you can.
beats.speak: An early queen attack looks frightening, but it is easy to meet. Guard F seven, keep developing, and chase the queen with your pieces when you can.

beats.label: Your turn
beats.say: Now try it yourself against the computer. Here Black threatens checkmate on f2. Stop the threat with a developing move, castle, and then chase Black's queen.
beats.speak: Now try it yourself against the computer. Here Black threatens checkmate on F two. Stop the threat with a developing move, castle, and then chase Black's queen.

practice.goal: Black threatens checkmate on f2. Stop it with a developing move, castle, and chase the early queen.

checkpoints.label: Stop the mate with a developing move

hints: Black's queen and bishop both aim at f2. Bring out a piece you have not moved yet so that it guards f2 or blocks the queen's line to it.
Look at your knight on g1, which has not moved yet. Which of its squares blocks the queen, and which guards f2?
practice.offTrack: That move does not stop the threat: Black's queen takes on f2 with checkmate. Undo it and guard f2 or block the queen with a piece you have not moved yet.

mistakes.d1e2: Your queen now guards f2, so the mate is stopped, but this lesson asks for a developing move. Undo it and bring out a piece that has not moved yet.
mistakes.d1f3: Your queen blocks the line to f2, but bringing her out early is the habit this lesson warns against. Undo it and stop the threat with a developing move.
mistakes.d1h5: Moving your queen frees d1 for your king, but Black's queen still takes on f2 with check. Undo it and guard f2 with a developing move.
mistakes.d1g4: Moving your queen frees d1 for your king, but Black's queen still takes on f2 with check. Undo it and guard f2 with a developing move.
mistakes.e1e2: Your king steps off the line, but it can never castle now and it stands in the open. Undo it and stop the threat with a developing move.
mistakes.f2f3: The pawn blocks the queen, but it develops nothing and takes f3 away from your knight. Undo it and stop the threat with a developing move.
mistakes.f2f4: This pawn move develops nothing, and the pawn can simply be captured. Undo it and stop the threat with a developing move.

lessons.title: The Fork
teaches: A fork is one piece attacking two enemy pieces at the same time.
The opponent can usually save only one of the two.
Knights are famous for forks, because their jump cannot be blocked.
Pawns and queens fork too; a pawn fork is strong because the pawn is worth so little.
A fork with check is usually strongest: unless the forking piece can be captured, the check must be answered first.

beats.label: Two targets at once
beats.say: A fork is one piece attacking two enemy pieces at the same time. The opponent can usually save only one of them.
beats.speak: A fork is one piece attacking two enemy pieces at the same time. The opponent can usually save only one of them.

beats.label: The knight's jump
beats.say: Knights are the champions of the fork. A knight's jump cannot be blocked, and its L-shaped attacks are easy for the opponent to overlook.
beats.speak: Knights are the champions of the fork. A knight's jump cannot be blocked, and its L-shaped attacks are easy for the opponent to overlook.

beats.label: Knight fork with check
beats.say: White's knight lands on e7. It checks the king on g8 and attacks the rook on c8 at the same moment.
